articles.title: Woman's Hour - Melania Trump's diplomacy, Philippa Gregory’s The Royal Witch, Back to Black at 20, Iron deficiency - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: What influence can a first lady have on world affairs?
articles.body: According to the White House, Melania Trump has taken on an unexpected diplomatic role. It's been reported that she helped to broker a temporary ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. The agreement, due to come into effect today, is intended to allow humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky and enable civilians to leave. But how did Melania Trump become involved? Why has she been sucessful and what does this tell us about the influence a First Lady can have on world affairs? Nuala McGovern is joined by Victoria Vdovychenko from the University of Cambridge's Centre for Geopolitics, and Anne McElvoy from Politico. Philippa Gregory is one of the world’s bestselling historical novelists. Her books have reimagined the lives of powerful and often overlooked women from Britain’s past. She joins Nuala to discuss her latest novel, Royal Witch, which tells the story of Eleanor Cobham, an ambitious noble woman in the court of Henry V who used astrology and other "dark arts" in her attempt to gain power. Twenty years after the release of Back to Black, Amy Winehouse's era-defining album continues to resonate. A five-time Grammy winner, it produced five hit singles and established Amy as one of the most distinctive voices of her generation. Dr Lucy O'Brien, author of She Bop: The Definitive History of Women in Popular Music, and journalist and music critic Jude Rogers discuss the album’s lasting impact and celebrate Amy's enduring legacy. How is iron deficiency diagnosed in the UK? And what impact do the effects of pregnancy, menstruation, and inflammatory conditions have? Nuala is joined by Dr Aziza Sesay, a GP who specialises in women's health and by BBC News reporter Zara Salaria, who has been looking into whether social media videos about "Ferritin face" have any scientific basis. Presenter: Nuala McGovern Producer: Helen Fitzhenry

articles.title:
Trump diz que vai proibir o termo inteligência artificial
 | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente dos EUA considera o termo impreciso e defende que a tecnologia passe a ser chamada de ‘superinteligência’; declaração foi publicada na rede Truth Social.
articles.summary: Presidente dos EUA considera o termo impreciso e defende que a tecnologia passe a ser chamada de ‘superinteligência’; declaração foi publicada na rede Truth Social.
articles.body:
O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou nesta terça-feira (27) que pretende proibir o uso da expressão “inteligência artificial” em documentos oficiais e em outros contextos.

Ele defende que a tecnologia passe a ser chamada de “superinteligência” , por considerar o termo atual impreciso.

A declaração foi publicada por Trump na rede social Truth Social, em uma crítica ao jornal americano The Wall Street Journal. O presidente questionou por que o veículo ainda utiliza a expressão “inteligência artificial” em vez de “superinteligência”.

“Em pouco tempo, vamos proibir oficialmente o termo ‘IA/inteligência artificial’ em todos os documentos relevantes, e em tudo o mais, devido à sua imprecisão”, escreveu Trump.

Inteligência artificial (IA) é o nome usado para tecnologias capazes de executar tarefas que normalmente exigiriam habilidades humanas, como interpretar textos, reconhecer imagens e produzir conteúdo. A expressão abrange diferentes sistemas, incluindo ferramentas generativas como o ChatGPT.

Já “superinteligência” é um termo associado à ideia de uma inteligência artificial que ultrapassaria as capacidades cognitivas humanas. Não é um sinônimo técnico consolidado para todas as ferramentas de IA disponíveis atualmente.

A declaração de Trump não detalha como a eventual proibição funcionaria, quais documentos seriam afetados nem quando a mudança entraria em vigor.

O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, durante conversa com jornalistas em 20 de outubro de 2026 — Foto: REUTERS/Kevin Lamarque

articles.title: Governo Milei diz que não comentará vitória de Lula | G1
articles.standfirst: Javier Milei foi o único líder da América do Sul que não parabenizou Lula pela reeleição. Para justificar silêncio, porta-voz presidencial alegou que presidente brasileiro não parabenizou Javier Milei, quando ele foi eleito em 2023.
articles.summary: Javier Milei foi o único líder da América do Sul que não parabenizou Lula pela reeleição.
articles.body:
O governo argentino indicou nesta segunda-feira (27) que não parabenizará o presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva por sua vitória nas eleições, segundo noticiou a imprensa argentina.

Segundo o jornal "Clarín", o porta-voz presidencial, Adrián Ravier, declarou que o governo argentino tomou conhecimento do resultado eleitoral, mas não pretende divulgar nenhum comunicado oficial, nem mesmo por meio do Ministério das Relações Exteriores.

O porta-voz alegou que Lula não parabenizou Milei, quando o argentino foi eleito em 2023: "Não houve nenhum gesto do presidente Lula para cumprimentá-lo [Milei] pessoalmente, nem nada do tipo. Por enquanto, não há nenhum comunicado que pretendamos divulgar”. A declaração foi dada durante uma coletiva à imprensa argentina.

Em um publicação no X em 19 de novembro de 2023, Lula comentou o resultado da eleição, mas sem mencionar Milei diretamente.

"Desejo boa sorte e êxito ao novo governo. A Argentina é um grande país e merece todo o nosso respeito. O Brasil sempre estará à disposição para trabalhar junto com nossos irmãos argentinos", postou Lula na época.

Milei é o único líder da América do Sul que não parabenizou Lula

Milei e Lula — Foto: REUTERS/Tierney L. Cross e REUTERS/Diego Vara

Javier Milei foi o único líder da América do Sul que não parabenizou Lula pela vitória. Os demais líderes da região, muitos deles representantes da direita, reconheceram o resultado e felicitaram o presidente brasileiro reeleito.

Os dois países mantêm uma das relações comerciais mais importantes da América do Sul, com forte integração industrial e participação central no Mercosul.

➡️ Em 2025, o Brasil foi o principal destino das exportações argentinas, com mais de US$ 12,8 bilhões em vendas, e também sua maior origem de importações, com US$ 18,4 bilhões em produtos comprados, segundo dados do governo argentino.

A demora na comunicação se soma à lista de desavenças, desgastes e trocas de ataques mútuos entre os dois líderes. (Veja mais abaixo)

O líder colombiano Abelardo de La Espriella, que foi eleito com apoio do presidente americano Donald Trump e deu apoio público à campanha derrotada de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), declarou que não têm afinidade e são de lados opostos do espectro político. Em sua fala de reconhecimento do resultado, entretanto, estendeu a mão para que os países continuem cooperando .

Já o equatoriano Daniel Noboa afirmou que a América Latina tem inimigos em comum e desafios compartilhados em sua mensagem de parabenização. O chileno José Antonio Kast disse que ligou para cumprimentar Lula e afirmou que os dois países têm um futuro em comum.

A líder peruana Keiko Fujimori defendeu o fortalecimento da aliança estratégica entre os dois países, com ênfase na integração, na cooperação e no desenvolvimento sustentável da Amazônia compartilhada. Rodrigo Paz , presidente boliviano, por sua vez, parabenizou o brasileiro e destacou os laços históricos entre Bolívia e Brasil.

Todos eles foram apoiados por Trump em suas campanhas eleitorais e, hoje, compõe o Escudo das Américas.

🔎 O Escudo das Américas é uma aliança multinacional de cooperação militar, política e econômica liderada pelo governo dos Estados Unidos para combater organizações criminosas transnacionais e o narcotráfico

Além deles, os demais presidentes do continente que felicitaram o brasileiro foram:

Delcy Rodríguez, presidente da Venezuela;

Jennifer Geerlings-Simons, presidente do Suriname.

As reações contrastam com a postura de Milei, a única exceção da região.

Ele apoiou o senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) durante a campanha eleitoral e fez críticas a Lula nas redes sociais às vésperas da votação. O presidente argentino chamou o brasileiro de “ladrão corrupto” e o acusou de fazer uma campanha suja.

O silêncio de Milei ocorre em um cenário de avanço da direita na América do Sul e de aproximação de governos conservadores com a gestão republicana dos Estados Unidos.

Relembre as trocas de ataques entre Milei e Lula

Em agosto, na convenção nacional do PL, em São Paulo, que oficializou a candidatura de Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) à Presidência, Milei fez ataques diretos a Lula e ao ministro Alexandre de Moraes, do Supremo Tribunal Federal.

Durante o evento, o argentino chamou Lula de "presidiário" e Moraes de "lixo careca".

No dia seguinte, em uma entrevista a uma rádio argentina, Milei acusou o Brasil de liderar uma "campanha anti-Argentina" durante a Copa do Mundo.

Milei também disse que Lula enviou marqueteiros ao país para interferir nas eleições presidenciais de 2023 e apoiar o candidato Sergio Massa, que foi derrotado.

"Eles tiveram um papel muito ativo na campanha de 2023. Ou vamos esquecer que os assessores de Massa eram um grupo de brasileiros? Eu quis ver o meu amigo Jair Bolsonaro e não me deixaram. Aqui, no entanto, o ex-presidiário (Lula) veio cumprimentar a ré (ex-presidente Cristina Kirchner)", disse.

Na mesma semana, em entrevista à emissora argentina LN+, Milei voltou a subir o tom.

O presidente argentino afirmou que Lula é "ladrão", "corrupto" e "não é inocente" . Também voltou a questionar as decisões do STF que anularam as condenações do petista na Lava Jato.

Ao comentar a reação do governo brasileiro, Milei afirmou que não considera as declarações agressivas.

"Agressivo é que alguém roube. É muito mais leve chamar um ladrão de ladrão do que o próprio ato de roubar", disse.

Ele também afirmou que as ofensas foram "palavras espontâneas".

Após os primeiros ataques, o Itamaraty convocou o embaixador argentino em Brasília para manifestar o descontentamento do governo brasileiro. Ao mesmo tempo, chamou para consultas o embaixador brasileiro em Buenos Aires .

Em nota, o governo classificou o episódio como "sem precedentes". O chanceler Mauro Vieira disse considerar o caso grave, mas descartou, naquele momento, medidas mais duras, como a retirada definitiva de representantes diplomáticos.

Além disso, inicialmente, o presidente Lula evitou alimentar a polêmica. Ao ser questionado por jornalistas sobre Milei, respondeu: "Quem é esse cara?".

Dias depois, no entanto, ele endureceu o discurso e classificou como uma "patacoada" a participação do argentino no evento do PL . Durante um ato do PSB, Lula afirmou que não aceitaria interferências externas na política brasileira.

"Eu não falei nada, porque a minha relação é uma relação de chefe de Estado com o Estado. (...) Eu gosto do povo argentino e não vou ficar trocando coisa com aquela coisa."

articles.title: Dois dias após vitória de Lula, Tarcísio se manifesta pela 1ª vez, reconhece resultado da eleição e sai em defesa de Flávio | G1
articles.standfirst: Governador de São Paulo publicou um vídeo nas redes sociais nesta terça (27). Ele também criticou o processo eleitoral e defendeu a união da direita em uma oposição vigilante ao governo federal.
articles.summary: Governador de São Paulo publicou um vídeo nas redes sociais nesta terça (27). Ele também criticou o processo eleitoral e defendeu a união da direita em uma oposição vigilante ao governo federal.
articles.body:
O governador de São Paulo, Tarcísio de Freitas ( Republicanos ), se manifestou pela primeira vez nesta terça-feira (27), dois dias após a vitória de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) na eleição presidencial . (Veja acima.)

Em vídeo publicado nas redes sociais, ele agradeceu ao senador Flávio Bolsonaro ( PL ) pela campanha, criticou o processo eleitoral e defendeu a união da direita em uma oposição vigilante ao governo federal. Aliado de Flávio, Tarcísio atuou como cabo eleitoral do senador durante o segundo turno.

“A eleição passou, a eleição passou, mas não passam estas imagens. O povo nas ruas, vestido de verde e amarelo, tomado por um sentimento de mudança. Foram 60 milhões de brasileiros e a cada um de vocês, obrigado”, afirmou o governador.

No domingo (25), em uma disputa acirrada e marcada por uma virada inédita, Lula foi reeleito presidente da República ao obter 64.256.232 votos, contra 59.826.041 votos de Flávio Bolsonaro.

No pronunciamento, Tarcísio também agradeceu ao senador pela campanha. “Obrigado pelo esforço, pelo entusiasmo, pela esperança. Obrigado Flávio por caminhar com a gente, foi incrível essa caminhada”, disse.

O governador e candidato à reeleição Tarcísio de Freitas (Republicanos) durante agenda em SP em 26/8/2026 — Foto: RODILEI MORAIS/FOTOARENA/FOTOARENA/ESTADÃO CONTEÚDO

O governador afirmou que, apesar do fim da eleição, permanecem os desejos de mudança manifestados pelos eleitores da direita. Entre as pautas citadas por ele estão o corte de gastos públicos, a redução de impostos, o incentivo ao empreendedorismo e o combate ao crime.

Tarcísio também criticou a condução do processo eleitoral e citou o que chamou de “uso da máquina”, lançamento de programas fora do prazo e “interferência do Judiciário”. “Reconhecer o resultado não significa calar sobre os excessos”, declarou, sem apresentar detalhes ou provas para sustentar as acusações no trecho publicado.

O governador ainda afirmou que a eleição deixou o país dividido e defendeu que a direita se una para fiscalizar o próximo governo. Segundo ele, o resultado das urnas deu ao seu grupo político uma responsabilidade, além de força no Congresso Nacional e nos estados.

“Agora é hora de unidade, de uma oposição vigilante, que cobre responsabilidade fiscal, que proponha aquilo que melhora a vida das pessoas e que fiscalize de perto quem governa pelos próximos quatro anos”, disse.

Tarcísio também afirmou que o Congresso terá papel fundamental na pacificação do país e no aperfeiçoamento do sistema político e das instituições, incluindo o Judiciário.

Ao final da mensagem, o governador disse que continuará trabalhando em São Paulo e que o estado seguirá fazendo entregas e atendendo à população. “Vamos fazer a nossa parte, pelas pessoas e pelo Brasil. A eleição passou, o Brasil continua”, concluiu.

Flávio Bolsonaro participou de almoço com prefeitos em SP e o governador Tarcísio de Freitas — Foto: Roberto Sungi/Ato Press/Estadão Conteúdo

articles.title: Morte de professor em Campinas gera onda de homenagens nas redes | G1
articles.standfirst: Amigos, colegas e ex-alunos prestaram homenagens a Alexandre Lippaus Rocha, que morreu após passar mal enquanto trabalhava em uma escola municipal de Campinas.
articles.summary: Amigos, colegas e ex-alunos prestaram homenagens a Alexandre Lippaus Rocha, que morreu após passar mal enquanto trabalhava em uma escola municipal de Campinas.
articles.body:
Alexandre Lippaus Rocha, professor de geografia que morreu após passar mal durante o trabalho em uma escola municipal de Campinas (SP), é homenageado nas redes sociais — Foto: Reprodução

"Um ser de luz", "a melhor pessoa que eu conheci", "um rapaz muito alegre e muito querido por todos". Amigos, colegas de profissão, ex-alunos e integrantes da comunidade escolar usaram as redes sociais para homenagear o professor de geografia Alexandre Lippaus Rocha, que morreu após passar mal durante o trabalho em uma escola municipal de Campinas (SP) .

Entre os relatos no Instagram do g1 Campinas , muitos destacam o impacto da notícia para quem conviveu om o professor.

" Xandão alegrava todos ao seu redor . Uma honra ter convivido contigo", escreveu um amigo.

" Um rapaz muito alegre e muito querido por todos , inclusive por mim. Que a família encontre conforto nesse momento difícil", publicou outro internauta.

Uma ex-colega relembrou os tempos de universidade. "Conheci o Alexandre quando fazíamos Geografia na Unicamp, sempre foi uma pessoa amável, atenciosa, engraçada e muito preocupada com todos ao seu redor."

Também foram frequentes as mensagens que ressaltaram a dedicação do professor à educação.

"Excelente professor, companheiro de coletivo e excelente amigo , os bons vão cedo infelizmente", escreveu uma colega.

"Um ser de luz, professor incrível! Vamos sentir muita, muita falta", publicou outra pessoa.

"Professor de verdade" , resumiu um comentário.

Um dos depoimentos mais emocionados é de uma pessoa que afirmou ter presenciado o caso na escola. "Eu estava lá, foi a coisa mais terrível. Os gritos de choro foi doloroso. A professora chegou pedir para fazermos uma roda de oração... eu mesmo tremi completamente", escreveu.

Ao final da mensagem, a pessoa definiu Alexandre Lippaus Rocha como "um anjo na terra" e "a melhor pessoa que eu conheci" .

Alexandre dava aulas na Escola Municipal de Ensino Fundamental e Educação de Jovens e Adultos (Emef/EJA) Oziel Alves Pereira, no Jardim Monte Cristo, e trabalhava na rede municipal havia dois anos.

Segundo a Secretaria Municipal de Educação, a escola chamou o Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu) e o Corpo de Bombeiros assim que o professor passou mal. As equipes foram até o local, mas ele não resistiu.

Em nota, a pasta lamentou a morte do professor e informou que a escola suspendeu as aulas nesta terça-feira (27 ).

Uma equipe permanecerá na unidade para oferecer apoio aos alunos e funcionários que precisarem de acolhimento.

articles.title: Câmara de São Luís derruba veto da Prefeitura à Lei de Zoneamento por 17 votos a 9 | G1
articles.standfirst: A prefeita de São Luís, Esmênia Miranda, havia vetado o projeto após a inclusão de 133 emendas pelos vereadores. Votação foi marcada por críticas à falta de diálogo entre Prefeitura e Câmara.
articles.summary: A prefeita de São Luís, Esmênia Miranda, havia vetado o projeto após a inclusão de 133 emendas pelos vereadores. Votação foi marcada por críticas à falta de diálogo entre Prefeitura e Câmara.
articles.body:
Presidente da Câmara Municipal de São Luís, vereador Paulo Victor. — Foto: Divulgação/Redes sociais

A Câmara Municipal de São Luís derrubou, nesta terça-feira (27), por 17 votos a 9, o veto integral da prefeita Esmênia Miranda (PSD) à nova Lei de Zoneamento, Parcelamento, Uso e Ocupação do Solo. A decisão ocorreu durante sessão extraordinária conduzida pelo presidente da Casa, Paulo Victor (PSB).

A prefeita havia vetado o projeto no dia 16 de outubro, após os vereadores incluírem 133 emendas na proposta original enviada pela Prefeitura. Segundo Esmênia, as alterações, inclusive nos mapas de zoneamento, modificaram o conteúdo do projeto elaborado após quase três anos de estudos e discussões com a população.

➡️ A Lei de Zoneamento, Parcelamento, Uso e Ocupação do Solo define como os terrenos e espaços urbanos de São Luís podem ser utilizados. Na prática, estabelece onde podem ser construídos prédios, casas, comércios e indústrias, além de determinar regras para a divisão de terrenos, limites de construções e ocupação de diferentes regiões da cidade. A atualização busca substituir normas da década de 1990 e orientar o crescimento da capital, considerando o desenvolvimento econômico, a infraestrutura e a preservação ambiental.

Durante a votação, parte dos vereadores defendeu a autonomia da Câmara para alterar projetos do Executivo e criticou a falta de diálogo com a Prefeitura. Outros parlamentares argumentaram que as emendas precisariam de estudos técnicos e novas audiências públicas, principalmente por envolverem possíveis impactos ambientais.

Vereadores criticam falta de diálogo com a Prefeitura

O vereador Raimundo Penha (PDT) votou pela derrubada do veto, mesmo afirmando que discorda de algumas emendas. Segundo ele, a Prefeitura deixou de encaminhar informações técnicas solicitadas pelos vereadores antes da votação.

“A prefeitura tem vários secretários que podiam vir até essa casa e dialogar. Então, o meu voto hoje é porque eu acho que a forma de diálogo precisa ser modificada. Eu não vejo inflexibilidade. Nós estamos aqui à disposição para o diálogo, mas isso não pode ser feito pelas redes sociais”, afirmou.

Penha também destacou que o Legislativo tem o direito de modificar projetos encaminhados pela Prefeitura.

“Os poderes são harmônicos, mas são independentes entre si. Dizer que um projeto que veio para cá não pode ser modificado é nos colocar não como vereadores, é querer que a gente seja auxiliar da prefeita. O parlamento municipal não é um órgão chancelador, ele é um órgão de discussão e é o órgão que vota”, declarou.

O vereador Wendell Martins (Podemos) também criticou a postura do Executivo. Para ele, a Prefeitura deveria apontar individualmente quais emendas apresentavam problemas técnicos ou jurídicos.

“Vamos discutir tecnicamente, pontualmente, cada uma das emendas, para vocês me mostrarem aonde que nós estamos ferindo constitucionalmente, aonde que a gente está tirando o dever e o direito de cada cidadão. Mas é muito mais fácil fazer um discurso aberto e dizer: está tudo errado, nada presta”, afirmou.

Já Beto Castro (Avante), eleito presidente da Câmara para o próximo biênio, defendeu que a atualização da legislação pode atrair investimentos, movimentar a construção civil e gerar empregos.

O parlamentar também reclamou da ausência de representantes da Prefeitura em reuniões convocadas pela Câmara.

“Onde é que existe diálogo entre duas pessoas se uma não quer? Não existe. Essa casa sempre esteve aberta ao diálogo com a Prefeitura. Muitas vezes, os secretários, quando a gente convida aqui para tirar dúvidas, sequer mandam um ofício dizendo que não vêm”, declarou.

Parlamentares questionam impactos ambientais das emendas

Entre os vereadores que defenderam a manutenção do veto, a principal preocupação foi a falta de estudos técnicos sobre as 133 alterações feitas no projeto.

A vereadora Thay Evangelista (União Brasil) afirmou que a Lei de Zoneamento terá efeitos sobre o futuro da cidade e que as emendas deveriam passar pelo mesmo nível de análise da proposta original.

“Nós estamos diante de uma legislação que impacta muito o presente, principalmente o futuro da nossa cidade. O Conselho passou mais de dois anos debatendo, com estudos técnicos, discutindo essa temática. Trouxe uma proposta e faço questão de enfatizar que não sou 100% a favor da proposta trazida, mas também compreendo que algo tão sério e tão delicado, que impacta tanto a nossa cidade, não pode sofrer alterações pontuais sem a mesma profundidade de debate e de estudo”, declarou.

O Coletivo Nós (PT), representado pelo co-vereador Jonathan Soares, também votou pela manutenção do veto. Segundo ele, algumas emendas podem contrariar leis federais de proteção ambiental, especialmente ao reduzir faixas de proteção nas margens de cursos d'água e modificar regras de ocupação de áreas costeiras.

“Algumas emendas que foram apresentadas vão contra o regime constitucional de proteção ambiental. Foram emendas que diminuem as faixas não edificáveis às margens dos cursos de água. Nós não podemos apresentar uma proposição municipal que contrarie a legislação federal. A nossa legislação não é superior à legislação federal”, argumentou.

A vereadora Clara Gomes (PSD) também questionou a falta de discussões públicas sobre as mudanças.

O vereador e deputado estadual eleito Douglas Pinto (PSD) afirmou que as emendas não passaram pelo mesmo processo de participação popular realizado na elaboração do projeto original, que contou com nove audiências públicas.

“Foram 133 emendas apresentadas que excluíram a participação popular. Isso é grave. A qualquer alteração na Lei de Zoneamento, a gente sabe que tem que ter a participação popular. A gente não é contra o desenvolvimento, mas quer que tudo seja cumprido de acordo com as regras, respeitando o meio ambiente”, disse.

Mudanças de voto e possibilidade de disputa na Justiça

Durante a sessão, o vereador Astro de Ogum (PCdoB) anunciou inicialmente que se absteria, mas depois decidiu votar pela manutenção do veto.

Ele defendeu um entendimento entre Prefeitura e Câmara e alertou que a falta de acordo pode levar a discussão à Justiça.

“Se não houver entendimento, ninguém vai chegar a lugar nenhum. Se não tiver um diálogo para resolver essas questões, não tem como. Vai ser sempre isso: vetos, projetos, leis não cumpridas. Eu acho que precisava ter entendimento para solucionar o problema. Agora vai para a Justiça, vai ser judicializado, e ninguém sabe quando vai ter um desfecho”, declarou.

Já o vereador Antônio Garcez (PP) mudou seu posicionamento inicial e passou a apoiar a derrubada do veto.

Após o resultado, o presidente da Câmara, Paulo Victor (PSB), determinou o encaminhamento da decisão à Procuradoria da Casa para comunicação oficial à Prefeitura.

Apesar da derrubada do veto, a legislação ainda poderá ser questionada judicialmente, principalmente em relação à constitucionalidade das emendas, às regras ambientais e à participação popular.

A Prefeitura encaminhou a nova Lei de Zoneamento à Câmara para atualizar as regras de crescimento urbano de São Luís, baseadas em uma legislação da década de 1990.

Durante a tramitação, os vereadores apresentaram 133 emendas, que receberam parecer favorável da Comissão de Constituição e Justiça (CCJ) e foram analisadas em blocos no Plenário.

Em setembro, o projeto foi aprovado por 21 votos a 1. Douglas Pinto (PSD) foi o único vereador a votar contra o texto final, por discordar das alterações parlamentares. Já o Coletivo Nós (PT) deixou o Plenário antes da votação por ser contrário à análise das emendas em blocos.

Ao anunciar o veto integral, em 16 de outubro, Esmênia Miranda afirmou que as mudanças descaracterizaram a proposta discutida com a população.

“Foram 133 emendas, ou seja, 133 alterações ao texto encaminhado. Com tantas mudanças, inclusive nos mapas, o estudo técnico foi descaracterizado. O projeto aprovado já não é aquele que a cidade discutiu durante quase três anos, por meio de nove audiências públicas em várias regiões da cidade e em quase 60 reuniões com a participação do Conselho da Cidade”, declarou.

Na ocasião, a prefeita informou que, caso o veto fosse mantido, enviaria novamente a proposta original à Câmara, permitindo alterações desde que acompanhadas de estudos técnicos, transparência e audiências públicas.

“Sancionar esse texto seria desrespeitar cada pessoa que participou dessa construção. Mas vetar não é parar. Agora, a Câmara vai analisar o veto, e tenho confiança de que os vereadores vão mantê-lo, em respeito a quem participou de todo esse processo”, afirmou.

Com a decisão desta terça-feira (27), os vereadores mantiveram o texto aprovado anteriormente, com as 133 emendas. O resultado representa uma derrota para a Prefeitura e mantém a possibilidade de uma disputa judicial sobre as novas regras de ocupação do solo em São Luís.

articles.title: Saúde em Caraguatatuba avança com atendimento mais ágil e redução de filas | G1
articles.standfirst: A Prefeitura de Caraguatatuba investe na reorganização dos serviços de saúde para agilizar atendimentos, reduzir filas e melhorar a assistência à população.
articles.summary: A Prefeitura de Caraguatatuba investe na reorganização dos serviços de saúde para agilizar atendimentos, reduzir filas e melhorar a assistência à população.
articles.body:
A rede municipal de Saúde de Caraguatatuba passa por mudanças na organização dos serviços, nos fluxos de atendimento e na estrutura das unidades, com objetivo de reduzir o tempo de espera e melhorar a assistência à população.

Entre as iniciativas está a implantação do Fast Track na UPA Centro, que registrou 1.154 atendimentos nas duas primeiras semanas de funcionamento, em julho de 2026.

Voltado a pacientes com casos de menor complexidade, o modelo registrou tempo médio de 22 minutos entre a entrada do paciente na unidade e a alta médica, segundo os dados da Secretaria Municipal de Saúde.

As mudanças também envolvem melhorias nas unidades de saúde e a integração entre as equipes médicas, de enfermagem e recepção. A proposta é organizar os fluxos de atendimento e oferecer um serviço mais ágil e acolhedor aos pacientes.

Sob a gestão do prefeito Mateus Silva, o compromisso é continuar avançando na qualidade dos serviços, reduzindo o tempo de espera e fortalecendo a saúde pública de Caraguatatuba.

A queda de pilastras deixou pelo menos cinco vítimas, na tarde desta terça-feira (27), no bairro de Pirajá, em Salvador .

articles.title: 'Moved back from Canada but now cannot wait to return': Redditor says homesickness drove him back home but Mumbai is not the same
articles.summary: A Redditor expressed concerns over the worsening AQI in Mumbai, where he was born and brought up and then came back to feeling homesick from Canada after
articles.body: A Redditor expressed concerns over the worsening AQI in Mumbai, where he was born and brought up and then came back to feeling homesick from Canada after living there for three years. The Reddit post went viral as he said he can't wait to return to Canada again after seeing the changed face of Mumbai, the pollution, the scarcity of open spaces to walk comfortably etc. The Redditor explained that there was no absolutely pressing reason for his return -- he only felt a bit homesick. But now he wants to go back. Such social media posts often rake in a lot of reactions, as many expats consult these groups before taking the decision to go back to India."I had a good job and a good life in Canada, with nothing much to complain about. However, I am more privileged here in terms of my living situation. We own homes, my parents have a separate home, and I own an apartment in a very good locality. Considering all these factors, I decided to move back," the Redditor said.But the city he called home changed and that shocked him enough that he is again considering returning to Canada and this time through Permanent Residency. "But after coming here, I feel that Bombay is not the same anymore. I am now considering returning to Canada next year with PR, and I am preparing for French to make that happen. However, I still find myself in two minds sometimes," he said."Whenever I step out, I feel like escaping. I really don't like the environment here. But when I am at home, life feels so comfortable. I have my own space, my assets, and a certain level of rootedness here," he said, explaining the duality of the situation he has been facing. "At the same time, I am alarmed by the recent developments in Mumbai, and I personally feel that things are going to get worse. However, when I see people around me living their lives normally, seemingly unconcerned about the AQI or anything else, I start questioning myself. Maybe I am exaggerating things in my mind. Maybe things aren't as bad as I perceive them to be.""Money isn't much of a concern for me. I can rent out my apartment, and my assets in India aren't going anywhere. I can return to Canada, work there, and build my life there.Is Mumbai really going to get worse? Should I focus completely on securing my PR and plan to leave as soon as possible, or am I letting my concerns about the city influence my decision too much?" the Redditor asked.'India is the best country if you don't get outside'The comment section highlighted how cities in India live inside gated communities and the outside world does not have much to offer. Many Redditors shared their similar experience of coming back to India from US, Canada, New Zealand and then moving out again. Many people, however, found the Redditor too privileged to be complaining about both Canada and Mumbai. "You moved to Canada and after 3 years moved back because you were homesick. A lot of us are homesick whether living away from home in or outside of India but we don't just get up and move. You now don't feel great because in 3 years you don't think Mumbai is the same anymore. Well! Just like anything and anyone else, cities too evolve and don't remain the same. articles.title: 'Funding cutbacks made Dunwich Heath wildfire more challenging'
articles.summary: Suffolk's chief fire officer Jon Lacey tells MPs the fire service needs more investment.
articles.body:
The chief fire officer for Suffolk has told MPs the summer wildfires have highlighted the need for more resilience and investment following fire service cutbacks.

Jon Lacey said tackling the fire at Dunwich Heath was "hugely challenging", with crews from 14 other services having to come to the county to help.

"We have seen cutbacks in recent years where firefighter numbers have been reduced and that proved challenging at Dunwich… national resilience and capacity should be looked at for investment," he said.

Lacey was giving evidence to the Housing, Communities and Local Government committee on Tuesday, in a one-off session on the current state of fire and rescue services.

The cross-party committee was exploring the arrangements the government needed to make to ensure fire services are better equipped to cope with climate change.

Lacey also spoke about the issue of rural services relying heavily on on-call firefighters, who also have day jobs.

He said: "You can only rotate them around a shift so many times."

He added that even then, many were being sent to "another fire or back to the fire at Dunwich only a few hours after they had just left".

His firefighters were also needed after Dunwich to help with blazes in Hampshire and Wales, "because we knew that they needed that help".

At the meeting, Lacey called for more funding.

"It is encouraging to hear that the RAF may well be providing us with firefighting capability [in the future], but that may come at a cost to local authorities," he added.

New technology, like robotics, could also make firefighters' jobs easier, but councils did not have the budgets to invest in that either, he said.

Referring to the prime minister's wildfire summit last week , the chair of the National Fire Chiefs Council, Phil Carrigan, said there had been positive signs about new investment in the country's fire service, but more was needed.

He also called for a better way of funding it in future.

Last week, Andy Burnham told reporters that fire and rescue services were "stretched" during the summer and firefighters had worked in "extremely difficult conditions", before committing to providing better equipment.

He said "too often in the past we've been playing catch up", adding "the summer we've just had is likely to be a more regular situation going forward".

articles.title: Sudan’s war steals children’s future with school closures and displacement
articles.summary: The conflict in Sudan has left millions of children without education, as they work to help their families.
articles.body:
Nine-year-old Abkar Mohammed works cleaning and polishing shoes on the streets of Port Sudan every day. He arrived in the eastern Sudanese city with his mother and three siblings from Khartoum days after the country’s armed conflict erupted on April 15, 2023.

Abkar lost his father before the war began and the family live in a rented a home in al-Kasara, a low-income neighbourhood in Port Sudan.

Due to the family’s financial situation, he doesn’t go to school but does attend classes at a traditional “khalwa” where he learns the Quran.

“When my lesson finishes, I pick up my shoe-cleaning equipment and head to busy areas to work,” he told Al Jazeera. “In the evening, I take public transport home, making sure I get back before sunset.”

He gets around 1,000 Sudanese pounds ($0.11) to clean or stitch a pair of shoes, and by the end of the day, he earns around 10,000 pounds ($1.08). He gives the money to his mother to cover the family’s daily needs.

“My 23-year-old brother works on casual jobs in the markets to cover most of the household expenses,” he said.

Abkar’s story echoes the lives of eight million of the country’s 17 million school-age children who are out of school, according to UNICEF.

In Darfur, one of the areas of Sudan hardest hit by the war, about 80 percent of schools remained closed with 70 percent of children in the area not attending classes.

Save the Children estimates that children in Sudan have missed on average about 484 days of classroom learning since the war began in April 2023, due to prolonged school closures, fighting, displacement and damage to education facilities.

The Rapid Support Forces (RSF), which has been in conflict with the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) since 2023, has been accused of targeting schools and universities in drone strikes, along with other civilian infrastructure.

In September 2026, a drone attack on two warehouses in North Kordofan destroyed more than 330,000 school textbooks and other learning materials.

Sulaima Ishag, head of the Government Advisory Council for Women and Children, told Al Jazeera that children who live in conflict zones, such as Darfur and parts of Kordofan, are at greatest risk of permanently losing access to education. This can have a dire impact on their future, particularly for girls.

“[There are] cases of school dropouts and child marriage reported, alongside sexual violence. [Girls] face additional risks, including adolescent pregnancy and increased domestic responsibilities, which can further limit their chances of returning to education,” Sulaima told Al Jazeera.

“The absence of schools as safe and protective environments leaves children increasingly vulnerable to a range of threats, including child labour, early marriage, recruitment and use by armed groups, exploitation, sexual violence, trafficking and family separation. It also takes a significant psychological and social toll on children … [particularly those] from the poorest families … even in areas considered relatively safe.”

Eva Hinds, UNICEF’s head of advocacy and communication in Sudan, said that nearly half of all school buildings in the country no longer function as classrooms, due to war damage.

“Displaced children, many of whom have been forced to flee several times, face additional barriers, as repeated displacement disrupts their learning and separates them from teachers and classmates, often leaving them without learning materials or a safe place to study,” Hinds told Al Jazeera.

Children who no longer attend school lose access to a safe space and are exposed to the risks associated with child labour, recruitment by armed groups, and other abuses.

Hinds warned that the longer children remain out of school, the harder it will become for them to make up for lost learning. This disruption can deepen existing inequalities and mean that a generation of Sudanese children and young people will be unable to contribute to the country’s future peace, recovery and development.

“The conflict in Sudan continues to have a devastating impact on children’s education. The consequences extend far beyond the classroom,” said Hinds.

Psychologist Hanaa Mohamed told Al Jazeera that prolonged displacement and interruptions to schooling have taken a significant psychological toll on children. Many are in a constant state of fear, experience sleep disturbances and have difficulty focusing.

“These pressures have also led to changes in behaviour, including increased aggression or social withdrawal,” she told Al Jazeera. “Being out of school deprives children of an important protective environment. The absence of that protection has also helped bring cases of violence and sexual exploitation against children to light.”

Sudan’s economy has been set back 30 years by the war, with 60 percent of Sudanese now living in poverty.

Families fleeing the conflict often enter new towns or camps where they have few social connections and sometimes are just carrying the clothes on their backs. Sudan’s dire financial situation means that there are few jobs available for adults, forcing parents to turn to their children for essential income.

Saliha Omer, who sells tea on a street in Port Sudan, said her meagre finances prevented her from enrolling her 11-year-old son in school.

He currently works at a grocery shop in Port Sudan, but Saliha plans to return to Khartoum in the coming days so he can attend school.

“I couldn’t enrol him because of our financial circumstances after we were displaced,” Saliha told Al Jazeera.

Mahmoud al-Ghali, 16, has not been to school since the war broke out when he was aged 13, and has been displaced several times during the war.

For the past three years he has sold sweets and crisps on the streets of Port Sudan to provide his family with extra income.

Mahmoud remembers his final days at school, when he and his classmates sat their end-of-year exams. They were preparing for intermediate school and a new chapter in their lives, but the war changed their plans.

“After reaching Al-Fao in December 2023, I worked as a street vendor until I managed to save some money. Then I came to Port Sudan with my uncle in July 2025, hoping to earn more so I could help my family with household expenses,” he told Al Jazeera.

Mahmoud buys packets of crisps or sweets from local shopkeepers and sells them on the streets. At the end of the day, he pays the trader back for the goods he bought and keeps the small profit of around 20,000 Sudanese pounds, less than $3 a day.

This hand-to-mouth existence and the constant financial pressure on his family, worsened by rising cost of living, means he also has little hope of returning to school.

But his two younger brothers have now returned to classes in their village in Gaziera State after the SAF regained control of the area. Mahmoud hopes to save enough money to expand his small trading business.

“I’ve got used to working because circumstances have left me with little choice,” he said. “I no longer feel as strongly about going back to school as I once did, but I’ll keep trying so my younger brothers can finish their education.”

articles.title: Florida manatee habitat ruling sent back to court after US wildlife agency changed the definition of harm under endangered species law
articles.summary: A US appeals court has sent a case over Florida’s wastewater regulations and manatee habitats back to a lower court after a federal rule changed the
articles.body: A US appeals court has sent a case over Florida’s wastewater regulations and manatee habitats back to a lower court after a federal rule changed the definition of harm under the Endangered Species Act. The lawsuit was brought by Bear Warriors United, Inc., against the Secretary of the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. The district court had ruled in favour of the Florida non-profit Bear Warriors United and issued a permanent injunction against the department. According to an opinion issued by the United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, the court vacated the judgment and injunction and asked the district court to assess the effect of the revised rule. The case concerns alleged damage to manatee habitats in the North Indian River Lagoon.Why Bear Warriors United sued Florida’s environmental regulatorBear Warriors United, Inc., sued the Secretary of the Florida Department of Environmental Protection, alleging that the department’s wastewater regulatory scheme damaged manatee habitats in the North Indian River Lagoon and ultimately harmed manatees in violation of the Endangered Species Act.The district court ruled in favour of Bear Warriors and issued the permanent injunction it had requested against the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. The department challenged the decision before the United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit.The case concerned the relationship between wastewater regulation, damage to manatee habitats, and the federal law protecting endangered species.The legal definition of harm that shaped the original rulingThe Endangered Species Act makes it unlawful for any person subject to US jurisdiction to take an endangered species within the United States or its territorial sea. The law defines the term ‘take’ as harassing, harming, pursuing, hunting, shooting, wounding, killing, trapping, capturing or collecting a protected species, as well as attempting such conduct.At the time of the district court’s judgment, regulations issued by the US Fish and Wildlife Service further defined harm as an act that actually kills or injures wildlife. The definition could include significant habitat modification or degradation when it killed or injured wildlife by significantly impairing essential behavioural patterns, including breeding, feeding or sheltering.The district court relied on this definition when concluding that Florida’s environmental regulator had violated the law.Why did a change in federal rules send the manatee case back to courtWhile the appeal was pending, the US Fish and Wildlife Service issued a new final rule rescinding the definition of harm on which the district court had relied. The change was published in the Federal Register on 14 July 2026 under the title Rescinding the Definition of “Harm” Under the Endangered Species Act.The new rule changed the regulatory framework relevant to the district court’s decision. The appeals court determined that the case needed to return to the lower court for further consideration.The ruling did not establish a new finding that the Florida Department of Environmental Protection had complied with the Endangered Species Act. Instead, the court vacated the existing judgment and injunction and directed the district court to evaluate the effect of the new federal rule on the case.Appeals court vacates ruling and sends manatee case back to lower courtThe Eleventh Circuit considered two appeals filed by the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. The first appeal was dismissed because it had been filed before the district court entered the requested injunction. At that stage, the case did not have a final decision suitable for appeal.The court had jurisdiction over the second appeal, which challenged both the judgment and the injunction. It then vacated both decisions and remanded the case to the district court.The appeals court’s decision was issued on 8 October 2026. articles.title: Hegseth heads to Manila to shore up US ties with Asia-Pacific partners
articles.summary: The Iran war and Trump’s criticisms of allies have led Asia-Pacific countries to recalibrate their calculations.
articles.body:
US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth will attend a Southeast Asian defence meeting this week alongside his counterparts from India, South Korea and Japan as Washington looks to solidify ties with the region after a year overshadowed by the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran.

The meeting will bring together defence officials from the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) plus eight of the bloc’s dialogue partners.

Australia, New Zealand, Russia and China are also expected to send representatives to the talks, which run from Wednesday to Thursday in the Philippines.

Known as the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus), the meeting will be held alongside a parallel ASEAN members-only event for Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Timor-Leste, and Vietnam.

India is among the dialogue partners that will host bilateral meetings on the sidelines of ADMM-Plus to “review the ongoing defence ties and explore ways to further strengthen strategic partnerships”, according to state media.

William Yang, senior analyst for Northeast Asia at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera that the focus will be on regional security concerns like Myanmar’s ongoing civil war and maritime disputes between ASEAN states and neighbouring China.

“The South China Sea dispute is going to be front and centre because the Philippines is the chair of this year’s summit,” he told Al Jazeera, adding that he expects Manila to push for ASEAN to finalise a code of conduct with China to outline how to approach maritime disputes and handle conflicts in the globally important waterway.

The Philippines, China, Vietnam, Malaysia, Brunei, and Taiwan all have overlapping territorial claims to the South China Sea, although Beijing claims most of it as domestic waters.

These disputes often leave Beijing at odds with its neighbours, and particularly Manila, as both sides claim the uninhabited Scarborough Shoal and parts of the Spratly Islands.

Tensions escalated sharply this month with at least “eight close encounters” in the South China Sea and nearby Luzon Strait, according to the US Naval Institute.

The spat turned into a war of words when Chinese Ambassador to the Philippines Jing Quan said Beijing could “easily win” a war with the Philippines, prompting a Philippine senator to call for his expulsion.

Beijing has yet to confirm whether Chinese Defence Minister Dong Jun will attend ADMM-Plus in person, but he could still make a last-minute appearance. The Chinese defence chief attended ADMM-Plus 2024 and 2025, according to Bonnie Glaser, managing director of the German Marshall Fund’s Indo-Pacific Program, and Hegseth’s presence could factor into Beijing’s calculations.

China and the US have spent the past year thawing their relationship. A face-to-face meeting between Hegseth and Dong could also lay the groundwork for two meetings between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping scheduled for later this year, following two previous meetings between Trump and Xi this year.

“It is certainly possible that he will attend again this year,” Glaser told Al Jazeera by email. “I would not be surprised if Dong meets with Secretary Hegseth, especially since China has repeatedly said that it attaches importance to strengthening crisis communications and preventing crises between the US and Chinese militaries.”

Analysts, however, say that the bulk of Hegseth’s work at ASEAN will be reassuring the bloc and its dialogue partners that the US remains committed to the region amid its months-long conflict with Iran.

The US has raised eyebrows in Asia over the past year by moving some of its military assets from South Korea and Japan to the Middle East, while Trump has also sent mixed signals on his views on Taiwan, another potential flashpoint for the region.

Trump has reportedly delayed a major arms package to Taiwan, an unofficial US ally, ahead of an upcoming meeting with Xi at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in November, before the Group of 20 (G20) Leaders’ Summit in December.

“What Hegseth says and does will be interesting,” said Ja Ian Chong, a political scientist at the National University of Singapore, because of recent comments by US defence official Elbridge Colby suggesting that Washington would focus less on empty gestures and more on substance in the Asia-Pacific region.

“How Hegseth keeps to these lines while trying to keep a US advantage will be interesting, since these are not easy calibrations to make,” Chong said.

articles.title: Israeli military detains Egyptian national who crossed border
articles.summary: Egyptian man held after crossing into Israel near Nitzana, his motive for the crossing still unknown.
articles.body:
Israel’s military has said that it detained an Egyptian civilian overnight after he crossed a border fence from Egyptian territory into Israel near Nitzana and that he was transferred to security forces for further questioning.

The military, which made the announcement on Tuesday, provided no additional details on the man’s identity, his motive or whether he was carrying anything at the time of his detention. Israeli state broadcaster Kan 11 reported that surveillance identified the suspect crossing the border and that troops were dispatched to the scene to arrest him.

Nitzana is a small community in southern Israel’s western Negev (Naqab) Desert, sitting directly adjacent to the Egyptian border opposite the Egyptian side’s Al-Awja area. The Nitzana border crossing, also known as the Eliav crossing, primarily handles cargo transport between the two countries rather than serving as a major passenger channel. It lies roughly 75km (47 miles) south of Beersheba.

The incident occurred as Israel maintains heightened alert levels along the Egyptian border. Israeli outlet Ynet reported that the military was treating the incident seriously and that it was under investigation.

Egyptian officials have not publicly commented on the detention.

Drug and arms smuggling takes place across the border between Egypt and Israel, neighbouring countries that signed a peace treaty in 1979 but whose relationship remains largely chilly.

Ynet reported the crossing came less than a year after Israel’s defence minister ordered the area adjacent to the Egyptian border declared a closed military zone and announced changes to open-fire regulations following earlier smuggling activity.

articles.title: Israel election turnout highest in 50 years as voting continues
articles.summary: Voting numbers by 6pm local time had exceeded the number of all votes in 2022 elections.
articles.body:
Two-thirds of Israeli voters had cast a ballot by early evening on Tuesday, according to Israel’s Central Elections Committee, exceeding the total number of voters at the last election.

By 6pm (16:00 GMT), some 66.7 percent of eligible Israelis had voted, up from 57.7 percent by the same time in 2022. Israel’s military says turnout among soldiers had climbed beyond 68 percent by 5pm (15:00 GMT) – higher than the 65 percent tracked at the same stage of the 2022 election.

Polling stations will close at 10pm local time (20:00 GMT), but the Central Elections Committee says anyone waiting in line at that time will still be allowed to vote.

This comes as local media reports say the committee rejected a request by Likud to extend voting hours beyond 10pm.

Israel’s far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has issued an 11th-hour appeal for right-wing voters to cast their ballots, saying that turnout “in the Arab sector is unprecedented” and that a “dangerous left-wing government” could take power.

“Do not despair! It is still possible to win,” Smotrich said in a post on X.

Prominent politicians from Arab-led lists have accused right-wing figures of incitement against Palestinian citizens, who make up 20 percent of Israel’s population, and of questioning their legitimacy to vote.

Mitchell Barak, a pollster and former aide to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, earlier told Al Jazeera that voter turnout “is really high and that’s good”.

“I think … it will probably pass its historic peak in ‘73 – when Israel was also involved in a huge war – so draw what conclusion from that you will,” he added.

The election is largely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s handling of the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks and the wars that followed, the most intense period of combat for Israel since the 1973 surprise military campaign by Egypt and Syria.

“Those numbers are going to help the incumbent parties,” Barak said, “as the 3.25 percent threshold a party needs to get into the Knesset remains, the number of votes you need to meet that threshold increases dramatically.”

Israeli officials noted that several polling stations had faced exceptionally long lines, which were attributed to high voter turnout despite rainy and blustery weather in parts of the country, and a flood warning in some areas.

In a message more than five hours after polls opened, Netanyahu urged supporters to vote, saying turnout was high among his opponents on the left and among Palestinian citizens of Israel.

“We need it to be high too. You all need to stream to the polls,” he said. “This is a fateful moment.”

Netanyahu had repeatedly warned supporters of the prospect of high turnout among Palestinian citizens in Israel ahead of the vote, seeking to mobilise his base under the slogan “the right or Palestine”.

Those voters were casting ballots in “unprecedented” numbers, Palestinian candidate Ahmad Tibi said.

Netanyahu and his main rival Gadi Eisenkot have ruled out partnering with Arab parties, citing a lack of shared values, although some possible scenarios envision them propping up a minority government to ensure Netanyahu is removed from office.

Meanwhile, an Israeli rights group has filed a complaint with the country’s election committee warning that widespread delays could be suppressing the vote among Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Though delays could be a result of high voter turnout, the Association for Civil Rights in Israel (ACRI) said in its complaint to the Central Elections Committee that delays had been reported in at least 18 communities. It asked the committee to investigate “whether these delays are deliberate”.

The ACRI also reported “a large presence” of police and National Guard officers at a polling station in the Negev Desert, raising concerns that officers were using crowd control as a pretext to prevent people from entering to vote.

Some employees raised the issue of H-1B and PERM and said that the company should lay off H-1Bs instead of offering a voluntary exit package."If Microsoft is actively encouraging thousands of employees to leave, how should the public reconcile that with claims that the company needs foreign workers because it cannot find sufficient qualified talent in the United States? How can the company credibly maintain that it has not abused the PERM labor certification process if it is simultaneously trying to reduce its existing workforce while asserting that it needs immigration sponsorship to fill talent shortages? American workers deserve a transparent, evidence-based answer," one wrote, per the purported screenshot.One pointed out the 31% jump in Microsoft's net income in FY2026 and asked why the company was reluctant to invest in people.H-1B and Green Card row of MicrosoftMicrosoft does not have an H-1B problem as the H-1B visa program is for temporary workers. The US government suspended Microsoft from sponsoring permanent residency for foreign workers. The administration accused Microsoft of Green Card fraud implying that the company is sponsoring Green Cards for employees who replaced Americans.Microsoft rejected the allegations and said it has a rigorous process to pick people for H-1B and PERM. "Of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications we submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees. These were not to hire new people. The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country," the company said."Microsoft only files H-1B petitions for those who meet the rigorous standards of this visa category. articles.title: Sudan war: West warns of famine risk
articles.summary: Millions face acute hunger in Sudan as conflict, drought and funding cuts aggravate the humanitarian crisis.
articles.body:
The US and 30 other Western states have warned of an "alarming deterioration" in food security in Sudan, urging the warring sides in the civil war to remove obstacles to humanitarian aid to prevent famine.

In a joint statement, the signatories said conflict was the main driver of Sudan's hunger crisis, damaging critical infrastructure and disrupting food production.

"There is very little to survive on," Yusuf Roble, regional director for Islamic Relief East Africa, told BBC Newsday, describing how people returning to Omdurman were finding their homes destroyed or looted.

The war, which began in April 2023, has displaced 14 million people.

The statement was signed by EU states, the UK, Canada, Switzerland and Norway, as well as the US, where it was published by the state department on Monday after first appearing on the European Civil Protection and Humanitarian Aid Operations website.

It estimates that 19.5 million people or 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity, including five million facing emergency levels of hunger.

"I met a mother of seven children who doesn't really know the whereabouts of her husband for the last three and a half years and he was the breadwinner, the sole breadwinner for the family," Roble said.

While the war in Sudan has led to what the World Health Organization has described as the world's worst humanitarian crisis, Roble said only 40% of Sudan's 2026 humanitarian needs plan had been funded as of September.

"Their meals come from the community kitchen, which doesn't really even have very long-term support because of funding cuts," Roble added.

The joint statement warns that "the number of children suffering from severe acute malnutrition could exceed the projected 825,000" without immediate action.

The crisis is being exacerbated by what the signatories describe as systematic obstruction of aid and the effects of El Niño, which has reduced rainfall and increased drought across more than half of Sudan.

"The parties to the conflict bear primary responsibility for alleviating the suffering of the Sudanese people," the statement says, urging them to lift all impediments to humanitarian assistance and allow full, safe, rapid and unimpeded access.

In June, the UN-backed Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, a measure of the severity and magnitude of food crises, estimated that 5.1 million people in Sudan faced severe hunger.

The civil war in Sudan began in April 2023 following a power struggle between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces.

articles.title: Death toll from attack by gunmen in northeastern Nigeria rises to 62
articles.summary: Bandits targeted Binnari village in Taraba state, setting fire to homes, shops, food supplies and motorcycles.
articles.body:
The death toll from an attack carried out by gunmen on a remote village in northeastern Nigeria has risen to at least 62, the country’s national emergency agency has confirmed.

Ladan Ayuba, head of the National Emergency Management Agency in Taraba state, where the attack occurred, said on Tuesday that thousands of people had been displaced by the raid.

Bandits targeted Binnari village in Taraba on Friday, setting fire to homes, shops, food supplies and motorcycles, according to Amnesty International’s Nigeria branch.

Police warned that the death toll could rise.

“We still have men on the ground, and the more we recover bodies, we will put them in account,” Victor Mshelizah, Taraba police spokesperson, told The Associated Press.

Nigeria is in the midst of a security crisis that began more than 15 years ago when the Boko Haram armed group launched a rebellion against the government. Civilians are regularly attacked and kidnapped for ransom by bandits in the north of the country.

In a statement, Amnesty International Nigeria said the authorities’ efforts to protect civilians were inadequate.

“The Nigerian authorities continue to leave rural communities in some parts of the north at the mercy of gunmen that repeatedly commit atrocities with impunity,” it said.

“This attack must be investigated impartially, while survivors must be provided with adequate reparations. On the side of the authorities, issuing bland statements condemning these horrific attacks is not enough.”

Many armed groups in Nigeria control illegal mining sites. Profits from these operations have increased their power by allowing them to purchase more arms and recruit more members.

The situation has led to an increase in arms smuggling and violence across the country and the wider Sahel region, according to the Institute for Security Studies (ISS).

articles.title: Lula’s victory echoes across BRICS after fears of a Bolsonaro win
articles.summary: Lula’s fourth term may have spared BRICS an internal fracture at a time when Trump is trying to reassert US power.
articles.body:
When Brazil’s President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva scored his surprise election victory on Sunday, winning an unprecedented fourth term in office, his supporters were euphoric.

The joy they felt over Lula’s victory has echoed across large parts of the Global South – and could restore some hope to the grouping that has sought to give emerging countries a greater stake on the world stage, the BRICS alliance.

At a time when United States President Donald Trump is seeking to reassert US power and has cast BRICS as a threat to US interests, Lula’s victory in Brazil offers the alliance a measure of political reassurance, experts say.

A win by his rival, Flavio Bolsonaro , could have threatened Brazil’s commitment to the bloc, given his links to Trump and calls to reconsider the country’s role in BRICS.

Instead, Lula’s return gives the grouping one fewer reason to fear a retreat from within – as it continues to help forge a more multipolar future for a world dominated by the US.

As Esmat Zaidan, professor of public policy at Qatar’s Hamad Bin Khalifa University, told Al Jazeera, “The victory of Lula is important to BRICS’ political continuation in the current climate as it seeks to increase the bloc’s role and make it stronger in global governance.”

It was clear to analysts that Lula’s win would safeguard the continuation of the BRICS alliance, while under Bolsonaro, its future may have floundered.

Lula himself was one of the architects of the bloc when it was founded nearly two decades ago, and has sought to advance its role on the global stage.

According to Zaidan, Bolsonaro’s desire to reconsider Brazil’s participation in BRICS and instead pursue closer alignment with Washington would have weakened the bloc’s political cohesion and potentially slowed cooperation on trade and financial reform.

Bolsonaro had reportedly also promised the US Trade Representative that Brazil’s Pix instant payment system would stay out of non-Western payment schemes, as the US seeks to safeguard global dominance of the dollar, said Imran Khalid, a geostrategic analyst and senior fellow at Foreign Policy in Focus.

“BRICS makes decisions by consensus, so one unwilling founding member can slow everything down from the inside. That was the real risk, more than Brazil walking out,” Khalid told Al Jazeera.

Still, Zaidan cautioned that continuity of the alliance does not amount to total unity within.

“The member countries of BRICS have distinctly different economic interests and geopolitical goals,” he said. “Therefore, while Lula’s victory makes it easier for the BRICS bloc to continue working towards a common agenda, his election did not eliminate these distinct differences.”

Guy Burton, a geopolitical and policy analyst, agreed that the bloc’s differences will remain unchanged with Brazil’s election result.

“BRICS matters because it represents a large share of the world’s population, economy and trade. But it has never really acted as a political unit. Its members are too different,” he said.

“The bloc now includes Iran and the UAE, which sit on opposite sides of the current war. That tells you how limited its cohesion is,” Burton added.

More multipolarity, but not a counterweight to Washington

The apparent relief in the Global South to Lula’s win reflects a broader concern among many emerging economies about their exposure to decisions made in Washington, “particularly regarding trade, tariffs and international economic relations,” said Zaidan.

“For these countries, the issue is not necessarily opposition to the US. It is about having greater room to make independent decisions and avoiding excessive dependence on any single global power,” he said.

Khalid pointed to China and Russia’s support for Lula, with Xi Jinping backing him against outside interference, and the Kremlin praising his work for the BRICS alliance.

“Most of these countries do not want a fight with the United States; they want the freedom to say no to Washington without being punished for it,” he explained.

“A strong Brazil inside BRICS helps protect that freedom.”

Lula has long advocated for a more multipolar international system, in which emerging economies have a stronger voice when it comes to shaping international rules and institutions, added Zaidan.

Burton said even countries and regions beyond the Global South are looking to lessen their reliance on Washington, including Europe, which is building its own security against Russia and in support of Ukraine.

“So states, whether in the Western camp or not, have accepted that they must pursue their own interests. That means working with whoever they can. We are moving into a genuinely multipolar world,” he said.

Still, BRICS’ diversity and its member states’ varied interests have meant it has never been a coherent counterweight to the West, experts said.

Many in the alliance maintain strong economic and security relationships with the US, said Zaidan.

“I would see Lula’s victory as strengthening the case for strategic autonomy rather than confrontation with Washington,” said the professor.

“BRICS is potentially more effective when it expands the choices available to its members, rather than defining itself simply through opposition to the United States.”

Burton agreed, pointing to Brazil’s changing ties with Trump over the years.

“Russia and China are the obvious US rivals. But India under Modi long had a close relationship with Washington, and with Trump in particular, even if that has weakened recently,” he said.

“Brazil, too, was close to Trump under Jair Bolsonaro, Flavio Bolsonaro’s father, when he was in office.”

Among the BRICS’ many ambitions is to promote trade in local currencies rather than the US dollar – and Lula’s victory could provide the political foundation to build on these efforts, said Zaidan, given that Brazil is one of the largest trading economies in the bloc.

Khalid said that after the alliance scrapped the idea of a common BRICS currency at its most recent summit in New Delhi in September, its ambition for trade in local currencies has become far more viable.

“If the [BRICS’ New Development Bank] moves towards its goal of 30 percent of lending in member currencies, and Brazil and China settle more trade in reais and yuan as they agreed in 2023, reliance on the dollar falls step by step, without an open confrontation,” he explained.

But Zaidan said that political will alone is not enough.

“Countries also need reliable payment infrastructure, sufficient currency liquidity, appropriate financial regulations, and businesses willing to use these arrangements,” he said.

For now the dollar reigns supreme in foreign exchange transactions, and there may be no tipping point for another decade or so, Burton said.

Ultimately, though, Lula’s victory could help BRICS move from political discussions towards more practical financial cooperation, while reducing dollar dependence will be “gradual, uneven and driven as much by economic feasibility as by geopolitical ambition”, said Zaidan.

How Washington reacts to this is another variable; Trump’s government sits at the contradiction of wanting to remain the world’s superpower, while also retreating to a more protectionist America-first role, said Burton.

“Developments such as Lula’s re-election will only sharpen the pressures already building in the Global North,” said the expert.

articles.body: India's defence industry is capitalising on Europe's growing appetite for ammunition as the Russia-Ukraine war forces countries to replenish military stockpiles and accelerate rearmament, opening a major export opportunity for Indian manufacturers.According to Defense News, citing Bloomberg-reported trade data, India's exports of ammunition and related products to European countries rose to $872 million in the four years following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, from $49.2 million in the preceding four-year period.Defence secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh had described India as Europe's third-largest arms exporter, highlighting the country's growing presence in the European defence market.The surge comes as European countries face pressure to strengthen military preparedness following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
