articles.title: The K-beauty products that Korean shoppers are actually buying
articles.summary: American and Korean shoppers are buying different brands when it comes to K-beauty — I asked a dermatologist to find out why.
articles.body: Korean skin care is everywhere right now, but not all K-beauty is created equal. Some of the viral products you see all over social media in the U.S. aren’t nearly as buzzy with Korean shoppers, which raises the question: Which K-beauty products are actually popular in Korea and why do they usually differ from bestsellers in the States? I spoke to Dr. Jane Yoo, a board-certified dermatologist in New York City, to find out. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. The best K-beauty products that are actually popular in Korea Below are K-beauty products that are actually popular with Korean shoppers, including recommendations from Yoo and bestselling products from Korean beauty retailers like Olive Young. I checked the retailer’s Korean websites to see the bestsellers that differ from the popular products on the store’s American website (more on that below). Best overall Yoo, who has eczema, participated in a U.S. clinical trial for this cream, and she says her skin felt and looked soft after applying it, and she even used it to soothe the blisters on her feet after running the Sydney Marathon. It has skin barrier-strengthening ingredients like ceramides and squalane, and has soothing vitamin E that’s great for sensitive skin, according to the brand. Yoo also loves using it after heavy-duty runs and workouts: “It was a godsend after the Sydney Marathon to use on my feet, which had developed blisters,” she says. Best serum This Torriden serum has a lightweight texture and is great for combination and dehydrated skin, says Yoo. The hyaluronic acid in the formula has a low molecular weight, meaning it has smaller molecules that help your skin absorb the serum faster and more effectively. It also includes panthenol helps to soothe redness and layers especially well underneath makeup, according to the brand. Best spray Anua’s PDRN collection is one of the most popular lines on Olive Young’s Korean website, and this hydrating facial mist is ideal for anyone looking to tap into the glass skin trend. The water-based spray has hyaluronic acid to moisturize your skin and PDRN, a popular K-beauty ingredient that helps boost collagen and reduce inflammation. You can throw this in your gym bag to hydrate your skin after a workout, or use it to freshen up throughout the day. Best sheet mask Yoo loves these cooling and hydrating sheet masks, which are made without alcohol or added fragrance. The masks are especially useful for soothing skin and reducing any puffiness or swelling, according to the brand. For best results, the brand recommends leaving the mask on for 20 to 30 minutes after cleansing. Best exfoliant This serum has spicules, which are small, needle-like structures that help ingredients absorb into your skin more effectively. They also increase cell turnover, which helps to improve texture and reduce the look of pores, according to the brand. The serum is mild enough to use daily, and has centella asiatica to calm irritated skin. It also includes exosomes, which help to carry proteins and lipids to your skin cells, making it especially helpful for issues like inflammation and fine lines. Best retinol This retinol serum is a bestseller on Olive Young’s Korean website, and includes pure retinol along with a peptide complex to help reduce the look of fine lines and pores, according to the brand. It’s also hypoallergenic, making it a safer retinol choice for those with sensitive skin, and has a thin, lightweight texture that makes it easy for your skin to absorb. Best moisturizer This cream made our list of the 100 best acne-safe products for its soothing ingredients, including niacinamide to help reduce breakouts and ceramides to keep skin hydrated. It also has soothing cica and tea tree leaf water, making it an excellent option for sensitive skin. Best toner pads Mediheal’s toner pads are gaining popularity in the U.S., but they’re already everywhere in Korea. These toner pads from the brand’s acne-care line are great for those dealing with stubborn breakouts. The thin gauze sheets are soaked in 98% pure madecassoside, which is a derivative of centella asiatica, that gently exfoliates. The pads are noncomedogenic (meaning they don’t clog pores) and are safe for sensitive skin, according to the brand. How I picked the best K-beauty from Korea I chose the products on this list based on the guidance given to me by Dr. Yoo, who suggests making the distinction between domestic bestsellers and what she calls “export brands,” along with paying attention to certain product types and ingredients. Brands: Yoo says it’s important to know the difference between “export brands” and the domestically bestselling brands that Korean consumers are actually buying in their day-to-day lives. Export brands refers to those that tend to dominate the social feeds and K-beauty conversations in the U.S. and Europe, like Cosrx, Medicube and Beauty of Joseon. I compared rankings from national bestsellers at Olive Young’s Korean website to the same list on its U.S.-based website, along with K-beauty top-seller lists from big beauty retailers like Ulta and Sephora.Ingredients: There are also specific ingredients that Yoo says are very popular in Korea right now. For example, PDRN (polydeoxyribonucleotide, a salmon-DNA-derived regenerative ingredient) is mainstream in Korea but still a niche, “trendy” ingredient in the U.S., says Yoo. Fermented ingredients like rice ferment filtrate and galactomyces, which is a fermented yeast, are much more embedded in everyday Korean skin care compared to Western skin care, she says.Product types: Products that are often seen as optional in skin care, like toner pads, ampoule treatments and sheet masks are also much more routine in Korea, says Yoo. “In the U.S., these are still read as ‘extra steps’ rather than staples,” she says. What’s the difference between Western and Korean skin care? The biggest difference between American and Korean skin care is the regulations, says Yoo. In the U.S., sunscreen is regulated by the Food & Drug Administration as an over-the-counter drug rather than a cosmetic like it is in other countries. “Korea regulates cosmetics including sunscreen as ‘functional cosmetics,’ which gives formulators access to newer, more photostable UV filters and lets them build lighter, more serum-like textures,” says Yoo. Although bemotrizinol (BEMT), a chemical sunscreen filter, was recently approved by the FDA in June 2026, “we’re still missing 10+ filters approved in other countries,” she says. The regulatory differences between the countries also explain the differences in approaches to and philosophies behind product formulations. “Korean formulation tends toward layering multiple lightweight products (essence, ampoule, cream, for example) to build hydration and barrier support gradually, while American formulations lean toward fewer products at higher single-active concentrations aimed at a specific concern,” says Yoo (for example, salicylic acid cleansers or vitamin C serums). Korean and U.S. ingredient lists are usually ordered differently or have varying names from country to country, so comparing products sold in Korea versus the U.S. may be misleading. “In some cases, the U.S.-market version is a genuinely different, reformulated product to meet FDA rules,” says Yoo. For example, the FDA recently approved Bemotrizonol (known as BEMT or Tinosorb S, internationally) as a sunscreen filter, which means U.S. versions of K-beauty sunscreens can now include it, though the international versions have already used it for years. Before this, Korean sunscreens sold in the U.S. had to change the formulas and replace the filter with approved ingredients like zinc oxide or avobenzone; now, the original Korean versions can be sold in-stores. Are the K-beauty brands popular in Korea different from the ones that are popular in the U.S.? Yes, the brands that are popular in Korea differ from the popular brands here, according to Yoo. “What trends on U.S. TikTok and [at retailers like] Sephora and Ulta skews toward brands built for export; they exist largely to serve international demand, and their marketing is built around that audience,” she says. The brands actually purchased and used by Korean consumers only somewhat overlap with the popular K-beauty brands sold in America, which is why it’s important to take what you see on socials with a grain of salt. “‘Popular in K-beauty content’ and ‘popular in Korea’ are related but not the same thing,” says Yoo. So, you shouldn’t treat U.S. TikTok trends as a read on Korean consumer behavior, she says. Dr. Jane Yoo is a board-certified dermatologist and Moh’s surgeon in New York City, along with a clinical assistant professor at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai and the founder of PLLC / Clinical Research Center of New York. articles.title: In 1969, a family purchased an Edvard Munch woodcut in Norway; 57 years later the rare print has resurfaced in England with a £50,000 to £80,000 auction estimate. Bidding is set for October 28
articles.summary: A rare early woodcut by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch, bought by a family in Norway nearly six decades ago, has resurfaced from a private collection in
articles.body: A rare early woodcut by Norwegian artist Edvard Munch, bought by a family in Norway nearly six decades ago, has resurfaced from a private collection in England. The artwork is expected to sell for between £50,000 and £80,000 at auction. The pencil-signed print, titled Melancholy III, was bought in 1969 and remained with the same family for 57 years before being identified for sale. Catherine Southon Auctioneers & Valuers will offer the artwork as a leading lot in its Fine and Decorative Art Auction on 28 October 2026. The print comes with its original sales receipt from Norway, which records the purchase price as 42,000 Norwegian kroner. It has remained in private hands since it was bought. Auction house records show that the print measures 37.8 by 47.2 cm and is printed on thick, cream-coloured wove paper. It has been kept in good overall condition.Rediscovery from a private estateThe artwork was found during a routine valuation by Catherine Southon Auctioneers. The family had kept the print in their home since the late 1960s. Its paperwork had been stored in a sideboard drawer with other household documents. Valuers identified the artwork as a very early print of Munch's 1902 woodcut Melancholy III. It is listed under reference numbers Woll 203 and Sch 144. The print uses shades of greyish blue and was made before the final version described in Gerd Woll's catalogue raisonné, a detailed record of an artist's works. Specialists noted that it was produced before the foreground figure was fully outlined and the background rocks were completely drawn. These details make it a rare early version of Munch's printmaking work.Heartbreak on the shoreline of ÅsgårdstrandThe scene in Melancholy is based on events in Munch's life during the summer of 1891 in Åsgårdstrand. This coastal resort lies south of Oslo, and Munch spent his summers there between 1889 and 1906. The image shows art critic Jappe Nilssen, a close friend of Munch, sitting alone on a rocky shore in deep sadness. Nilssen had suffered an unreturned love for painter Oda Lasson, who was married to artist Christian Krohg. In the background, two figures representing Lasson and Krohg walk along a pier towards a small boat, preparing to travel to a nearby island. Munch placed Nilssen in the foreground, bent forward in a pose similar to Auguste Rodin's The Thinker. His posture reflects feelings of loneliness, rejection, and emotional pain. Munch first created the scene as a pastel drawing in 1891. He later developed it in five oil paintings made between 1891 and 1896. Early versions were titled The Yellow Boat or Jappe on the Beach. Art historians widely describe the composition as one of Munch's earliest Symbolist works. It turns personal emotional pain into a landscape scene and came before his famous 1893 painting The Scream.Innovation in color woodblock printingMunch explored the scene through printmaking, experimenting with different textures and shades. He produced two distinct woodcut versions between 1896 and 1902. Melancholy III shows his early use of a complex printing method known as the puzzle or "jigsaw" technique. To make the print, Munch used two separate oak woodblocks. The colour block had no carved lines. Instead, he used a fretsaw to cut the wood into separate pieces representing the sky, sea, and shore. He applied different shades of ink to each piece, then fitted them back together like a puzzle before putting the block through a printing press. The second block contained the main outlines of the figure and rocky coastline. Munch carved these lines into the wood, covered the block with black ink, and printed it over the colour layer. Because he applied ink to each cut section by hand and experimented with different colour combinations, every print in the edition is different.Auction procedures and catalogue detailsThe print will be auctioned on 28 October 2026 at 10:00 BST at Catherine Southon Auctioneers & Valuers in Chislehurst. Bidders can take part in person, by telephone, or through online bidding platforms. Listed as Lot 160, the artwork has an estimated sale price of £50,000 to £80,000. Buyers will also pay a standard buyer's premium of 27.6 percent, including VAT. articles.title: Motorist led astray by GPS in Georgia stumbles upon house fire and saves sleeping family of 14
articles.summary: A large Georgia family survived flames that completely destroyed their house — thanks to a Good Samaritan who stumbled upon the blaze after his GPS took him a different way home.
articles.body: A large Georgia family survived flames that completely destroyed their house — thanks to a Good Samaritan who stumbled upon the blaze after his GPS took him a different way home, officials said Tuesday. Firefighters in northwest Georgia were called at 11:58 p.m. on Oct. 17 and rushed to 28 Rowlls Road, where they found the structure completely engulfed by flames, Lyerly Fire Chief Tim Deberry told NBC News. James and Larita Burke, their 11 adopted children and one grandchild made it out safely with a helping hand from 37-year-old motorist Casey Sparks, officials said. Sparks had been playing softball that day in Dalton, Georgia, and was headed home to Concord, Alabama, when his GPS kept putting him on Georgia State Route 114, a highway he had not used on the way up. “I redid my GPS like two or three times and it kept telling me to go that way,” Sparks told NBC News. “So it’s like ‘All right, I guess we’re going this way.’” A short time later, Sparks spotted flames near Lyerly, which is about 60 miles south of Chattanooga, Tennessee. “It was a glow, like a bonfire,” he said. “I mean you could see the glow from the fire from the hill.” Sparks rolled up to the scene and spotted a teenage boy fighting a losing battle against flames with a garden hose. “The whole front of the house had caught on fire, so there was no point in even trying to help him put it out,” said Sparks, a welding equipment repairman. “It was too far gone.” Before rushing into the house, Sparks said he told his 13-year-old son to call 911. Deberry said Sparks likely saved lives with his fast action. “He had actually come in, opened the door, started yelling, ‘Get out, the house is on fire!’ and started getting them out of the house,” the fire chief said. “If they would have been in there for probably no more than five more minutes, there would have been fatalities.” Sparks recalled spotting a little girl in a hospital bed, grabbing her and handing her to a neighbor outside. “I scooped her up and tried to go out the door that I came in, but it was completely engulfed,” Sparks said. “So I found another door and went outside and handed her over the fence and then went back inside to help get everybody else out. “ Sparks said he was never in fear during those tense moments, but working on adrenaline and trying to stay focused on the task at hand. “We’re from the South, man, and we help each other. We help our neighbors,” Sparks said. “I mean, I would hope somebody would do the same for me.” James Burke, 58, told NBC affiliate in Chattanooga WRCB that he’s grateful for Sparks and the motorist’s seemingly uncooperative GPS. “He was on the wrong road. His GPS put him on the wrong path,” Burke said. “He’s never been down that path before, and he said he knew that something was bringing him down that road when he saw the fire from the top of the hill; he knew he had to take action. I’m so thankful that he did.” Burke told the outlet he fell asleep in his recliner that night as the rest of his family were in their beds. He said he woke up to a stranger yelling at him in his living room. “The next thing I know, some guy was telling me in my living room, ‘Hey, you’ve got to get out of here. Your house is on fire,” he told WRCB. Sparks said he can laugh now at the frustration he felt in the moment on that late night of Oct. 17. Now Sparks believes a divine hand was working OT to put him on that road through Lyerly. “Now I see it, I wasn’t putting two and two together at the time,” he joked. “I was seeing we had three hours to drive and I guess we’re going this way.”

articles.title: Protesters storm Serbian pro-Vucic TV station after his loss at polls
articles.summary: President Vucic called the incident an attack on free speech and the freedom of journalism.
articles.body:
Protesters stormed a Serbian television station supportive of former President Aleksandar Vucic, interrupting broadcasting to call for the arrest of its editor, as tens of thousands took to the ‌streets for a second night of post-election celebrations late Monday after his defeat at the polls.

Live footage broadcast by Informer TV showed about 30 people entering its newsroom on Monday evening and surrounding editor-in-chief and owner Dragan Vucicevic. Some protesters shouted, “This is how it is in free Serbia!” and “Where is Vucic now?” Others called for Vucicevic’s arrest.

On his personal Instagram account, Vucic, dressed in a jumper displaying the crossed-out word “sorry”, called the incident an attack on free speech and the freedom of journalism.

Serbia’s Student List, born out of a student-led anticorruption protest movement, defeated Vucic’s alliance in a historic election on Sunday, bringing to an end his party’s 14-year grip on power. Vucic, who became prime minister in 2014 and president in 2017, previously served as information minister under Slobodan Milosevic and maintained tight control over the media during his rule.

Celebrations erupted across Serbia, with fireworks lighting the sky almost immediately after Vucic made an announcement conceding defeat.

“It means freedom from a dictatorship that has lasted for 12 years, that I cannot remember a time before,” voter Jana Vasic told Al Jazeera.

The student movement has no clear leader, and Serbians are waiting to see whom it will appoint as prime minister and to other key positions. The leading candidate on its election list, cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic , called for calm.

“We ask of you to stay calm and dignified until the end of the electoral process, just like you have been until now,” he said in a video posted on his Instagram account. “Don’t resort to any form of violence. Your Student List and your student movement urge you on this.”

The Independent Association of Journalists of Serbia said in a ‌statement ⁠that it would submit an application on Tuesday to have Informer TV’s broadcasting licence revoked, citing systematic violations of law and programme obligations.

Meanwhile, Informer’s Vucicevic released a statement saying, “On the very first day of [Student List] power, they want to ban the media. They have said everything about themselves, and nothing about us.”

In a separate development, a group of people also gathered outside the private pro-Vucic Pink TV station in Belgrade on Monday evening, which was cordoned off by police.

Earlier, public ⁠broadcaster RTV in the Vojvodina region began its evening news bulletin by apologising to viewers for failing to fulfil its role, citing uncritical, one-sided reporting.

Serbia was ranked 104th out of 180 countries in the 2026 World Press Freedom Index by Reporters Without Borders, its lowest position ever ⁠and worst in the European Union-Balkan region.

The Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability (Crta) election monitor said last week that television stations with national reach gave three-quarters of the time allotted to politicians to government representatives. The Student List was portrayed negatively more than 80 percent of the time it was discussed, Crta added.

articles.title: A grandmother's jewellery collection sat hidden in an English family attic for decades. When 201 lots went to auction, they fetched £506,750, more than triple their valuation, including a 1905 Cartier brooch
articles.summary: A forgotten jewellery collection that had been stored in boxes in a Worcestershire attic for decades has sold at auction for £506,750.
articles.body: A forgotten jewellery collection that had been stored in boxes in a Worcestershire attic for decades has sold at auction for £506,750. The final total was more than three times the original pre-sale estimate. The 201 individual lots belonged to a late grandmother from Malvern. Her family discovered the full collection while clearing out the loft of her home. Auctioneers had initially valued the entire collection at around £150,000. However, international buyers later competed fiercely for the pieces online and over the telephone. Chorley’s Auctioneers managed the sale at its Prinknash Abbey saleroom in Gloucestershire. Every lot found a buyer, giving the multi-hour auction a 100 percent sell-through rate.Standout pieces and international bidding warsThe most valuable item in the collection was a rare Belle Époque diamond and gemstone brooch designed by French luxury jewellery house Cartier. The piece dates back to 1905. The brooch features delicate openwork platinum settings, a style associated with jewellery made during the Edwardian period. It attracted strong competition from collectors around the world. Bidding quickly passed its original estimate of £10,000 to £15,000. It eventually sold to a private buyer bidding by telephone for £48,000, before buyer fees were added. Another major highlight was an early 20th-century necklace made with natural pearls and diamonds. The necklace had a modest initial estimate, but interest increased after laboratory tests confirmed that the pearls came from natural saltwater sources. Following competitive bidding from trade specialists in London and Geneva, it sold for £34,000. Other notable sales included a late Victorian sapphire and diamond cluster ring, which fetched £18,500, and a group of Art Deco diamond dress clips that sold for more than £42,000 combined.Decades forgotten in a Malvern loftAccording to statements released by Chorley’s Auctioneers, the late owner collected the jewellery throughout the middle of the 20th century. Many pieces had been passed down from older family members. Others had been bought from dealers in London and at regional estate sales. After her death, the jewellery was packed into its original leather presentation cases, biscuit tins, and velvet pouches. The items remained untouched in the attic of her Malvern home for decades. Family members found the collection while preparing the property for sale. They were unsure how much the dusty, tarnished boxes were worth, so they asked specialists from Chorley’s to inspect the items and value them at the property. While cataloguing the collection, specialists identified marks linked to well-known jewellery houses, including Cartier, Boucheron, and Garrard. They also found pieces without brand names from the Victorian, Edwardian, and Art Deco periods.Specialist reaction to the saleroom outcomeAuctioneers said the high quality of the jewellery and its well-preserved condition helped drive strong interest from buyers. Because the pieces had spent decades stored away from light and had not been worn regularly, many still had their original settings and gemstones that had not been polished. After the sale, Werner Freundel, director at Chorley’s Auctioneers, described the team's reaction to finding the collection and the excitement surrounding the bidding. "It was an absolute thrill to cataloguing such an extraordinary collection that had lain hidden for so long," Freundel said. "The late owner clearly had a fantastic eye for quality, buying pieces for their beauty rather than just as investments. To see the collection achieve more than three times its pre-sale estimate is a wonderful outcome for the family." Freundel added that collections from private estates that have not previously appeared on the market continue to attract strong prices. Collectors are especially interested in items with a documented history of private ownership. The total hammer price for the 201 lots reached £506,750. The proceeds will be distributed among the grandmother’s surviving heirs.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: Former Pretty Little Liars actress Shay Mitchell made a quick profit on her vintage Los Angeles home, selling the property for more than its asking price just three years after buying it. Public property records cited by the Los Angeles Times show that Mitchell sold the Spanish-style home, built in 1931, for $1.95 million (£1.27 million at 2015 exchange rates). The final price was higher than the original asking price of $1.895 million, following strong interest from buyers soon after the property went on the market. Mitchell bought the house in 2012 for $1.35 million. During her three years of ownership, she made a gross profit of $600,000 before closing costs and renovation expenses. The gain reflected both rising local property values and the extensive work she carried out to update the home's interior.Renovations transform classic Spanish designBuilt in the early 1930s, the two-storey home retains many features of classic Spanish Revival architecture. These include arched doorways, wrought-iron details, original tile work, and exposed wooden ceiling beams. According to property listings and reporting by the Los Angeles Times, Mitchell updated the interior while keeping its original style. She replaced dated decorations with custom finishes, modern light fittings, and dark hardwood floors throughout the main living areas. The 2,600-square-foot home has three bedrooms and three bathrooms. The main bedroom suite includes a renovated bathroom with modern fittings, as well as a private balcony overlooking the grounds at the back of the property. On the ground floor, French doors in the living room open directly onto an outdoor courtyard. This creates a living space that connects the indoors with the outdoors, making use of Southern California's warm climate.Kitchen and outdoor entertaining spacesThe interior renovations also included the kitchen, which was redesigned with custom cabinets, marble countertops, and upgraded stainless steel appliances. Outside, the property has a swimming pool and spa surrounded by mature plants and tall hedges that provide privacy. A patio for outdoor dining sits next to the pool. There is also a built-in fire pit area designed for entertaining guests. Property listing details show that the home includes a separate guest casita with its own bathroom. The extra space can be used as an office or a guest suite.Swift market turnaround in Los AngelesThe quick sale highlighted strong demand for renovated homes with traditional features across Los Angeles residential neighbourhoods during the spring 2015 property market. The Los Angeles Times reported that the property was listed in mid-April 2015 for $1.895 million. The sale was completed within weeks, closing in May 2015 at $1.95 million. The protests began as student-led demonstrations over teacher shortages and poor conditions at schools but have since evolved into a broader anti-government movement, with protesters voicing frustration over the cost of living and other grievances. articles.title: Serbia’s student movement topples Vucic’s party after 14 years, but political agenda remains unclear
articles.summary: Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to the Student List after a landslide victory ended his 14-year rule over Serbia in a historic election day.
articles.body: Serbia’s longtime leader, President Aleksandar Vucic, conceded defeat Sunday to the student-led opposition in an election that sent shock waves throughout Europe and the Western Balkans. "We do not have the final results yet, and many people will be surprised. Based on a stratified sample, it is clear that we have lost these elections. The student-led protest list has won," Vucic said in an address to the nation Sunday night. The Student List victory brings an end to 14 years of Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party rule, in what many are saying is the biggest political shake-up in the Balkans since the toppling of Yugoslav dictator Slobodan Milosevic in 2000. Observers say the Student List party's policies remain vague, which has some worried about Serbia's future. Ana Brnabic, vice president of the main Board of the Serbian Progressive Party, told Fox News Digital that, "The election victory of the Student List recalls similar electoral triumphs in other countries. The Student List represents a classical anti-establishment movement: it had neither a program nor a coherent political ideology. In an essentially anarchic fashion, it opposed everything, claiming to fight for justice and against corruption." ANTI‑CORRUPTION PROTESTS HIT EUROPEAN NATION AS CALLS FOR NEW ELECTIONS GROW She added, "After 14 years of Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) rule, people may have wanted change. That is understandable and logical. But the grim consequences of this movement in power will soon become apparent." Turnout reached 69 %, the highest this century, with more than 4.4 million people casting their ballots, according to Rasa Nedeljkov, head of the CRTA Election Observation Mission. "This is by all means a historic victory and indeed a surprise to many. While it was clear from the beginning that the students will have an impressive result, very few expected a landslide," Helena Ivanov, associate fellow at the Henry Jackson Society, told Fox News Digital. The Election Observation Mission reported that the Student List won 52.45 % of the vote and is projected to hold 138 of 250 seats in the National Assembly, an absolute majority, allowing it to form a government on its own. Vucic won 39.2 % and is projected to hold 103 seats. Supporters celebrated throughout Belgrade and across Serbia as it became clear the Student List won by a larger margin that caught many experts and observers by surprise. Many claimed they were concerned about the possibility of violence escalating as polls began to close. Almost two hours after polling stations closed, Vucic addressed the nation, confirming his defeat and announcing the peaceful transfer of power. FRANCE ROCKED BY STUDENT RIOTS AS HUNDREDS ARRESTED, VIOLENCE SPREADS NATIONWIDE "The path to an electoral victory with such a decisive margin will undoubtedly earn its own chapter in the handbooks on how to topple an autocrat. Two years of unprecedented grassroots mobilization, creative organization and impeccable campaigning kept the student list two steps ahead of the regime. Vučić was left playing catch-up, and all his attempts to co-opt, demoralize and fragment the movement failed," Sinisa Vukovic, director of the Global Policy Program at the School of Advanced International Studies at Johns Hopkins University, told Fox News Digital. The CRTA Election Observation Mission reported that the campaign was marked by the abuse of state resources, pressure on candidates and voters, attempts to bring the media under total government control, and attacks on independent election observers. Tens of thousands of Serbians volunteered to run and monitor polling stations across the country, and the vote was mostly peaceful. SERBIA, CAUGHT BETWEEN EUROPE AND RUSSIA, COULD MOVE ONE STEP CLOSER TO NORMALIZING RELATIONS WITH KOSOVO Student led protests marched in the streets for two years after the deaths of 16 people following the collapse of a railway station in the town of Novi Sad in November 2024. People had taken to the streets, demanding justice for those killed and accountability for anyone responsible for the disaster. The momentum of nearly two years of street demonstrations culminated in a nationwide movement ready for change. The political novices were able to rally the nation behind a simple message against corruption and state capture. Serbs across the country embraced the Student List, who are viewed as fresh faces in politics and are not tied to Serbia’s traditional political opposition, which is perceived as ineffective and corrupt by a lot of the voters. EXCLUSIVE: SERBIAN PRESIDENT VUČIĆ SAYS SUPPORT FOR US 'SURGED' UNDER TRUMP, INVITES HIM TO VISIT BELGRADE Milos Jevtic, a 48-year-old professor with the Faculty of Organizational Sciences at the University of Belgrade, was among the many Student List candidates who won a seat in parliament. Jevtic told Fox News Digital that their victory came from the values that the students have stood for from the very beginning: expertise, professionalism, responsibility, solidarity and unity. "What is particularly important is that the students have never compromised on these values and principles. Of course, widespread public dissatisfaction also played a major role, along with a lack of trust in both the current regime and the opposition parties," Jevtic explained. Jevtic said he believes the priorities for the new Student List-run government should be economic stability, fighting corruption, establishing the rule of law and strengthening institutions, much of what carried the student-led protests since 2024. "The ultimate goal is to build a system in which institutions function in the interests of all citizens," Jevtic said. On foreign policy, there is an expectation that there will be a certain degree of continuity with the Vucic administration in international relations, including maintaining good relations with neighboring European countries and all major international partners. But Brnabic warned that "Serbia has lost meaningful political pluralism. After 35 years of a multiparty system, the country is effectively left with one established political party, SNS, while the rest of the political scene is dominated by largely unknown movements without a clear ideology. This is catastrophic for any parliamentary democracy." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP She added, "Secondly, nobody in Serbia knows where the country is heading. Are we firmly pro-EU? articles.title: Arab parties in Israel accuse Netanyahu of inciting hatred to scare voters
articles.summary: In one social media post, PM Netanyahu accused Arab voters of ‘raiding the polling stations and stealing the elections’.
articles.body:
Prominent politicians from Arab-led lists have accused Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of inciting hatred against Palestinian citizens in the country, in an attempt to boost his electoral prospects.

Yousef Jabareen, leader of the Joint List, said in a video statement shared on social media on Tuesday that Netanyahu knew that “we can put an end to his bloody reign”. Meanwhile, Mansour Abbas, leader of the United Arab List, denounced Netanyahu’s comments as a “scare tactic to mobilise right-wing voters and drive them to the polls”.

In a series of posts on X on Tuesday, Netanyahu attacked Arab voters, describing them as “Muslim Brotherhood supporters” and accusing them of “raiding the polling stations and stealing the elections”.

In a separate post, Netanyahu referred to a picture of a large queue that appeared to show Palestinian citizens in Israel at a polling station, and called on right-wing Israelis to “go out and vote for Likud”, referring to his political party and describing the situation as a “matter of life and death for us”.

Adalah, the Legal Center for Arab Minority Rights in Israel, said on Tuesday that it had received numerous reports from Arab voters of attempts to discourage them from casting their ballots. Adalah said it had also been told that queues at polling stations in Arab-majority towns were moving very slowly and, in some instances, had stopped altogether. It also reported a lack of ballot slips printed in Arabic.

The rights group said it had reported the events to Israel’s Central Elections Committee and Regional Elections Committees.

Palestinian politician Sami Abu Shehadeh, who leads the Balad party, praised Palestinian citizens in Israel in a post on X.

“There are racists for whom these pictures are frightening, but for us, they encourage us and we’ll continue with all our might! I call on Arab citizens to continue coming out in droves, it’s in our hands!” Abu Shehadeh said.

Netanyahu has claimed that his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot , would be unable to govern without the support of Arab parties. However, Eisenkot has ruled out working with any, citing a lack of shared values.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: The ministry of civil aviation on Tuesday reviewed aviation safety and operational readiness as Cyclone Arnab is expected to intensify into a very severe cyclonic storm and cross the Andhra Pradesh coast on October 28, bringing winds of 125–135 kmph and gusts of up to 150 kmph, according to the India Meteorological Department (IMD).In a statement issued by the Press Information Bureau (PIB), the ministry said flights to and from coastal Andhra Pradesh and southern Odisha, including Bhubaneswar, were expected to be among the most affected. articles.body: Real Christmas trees fill the air with fresh pine scents and, depending on where you shop, buying them often supports local tree farms. They shed a lot, though, creating a mess that’s not fun to clean after the holiday season. If you’re looking to avoid the hassle of buying and maintaining a new one every year, an artificial Christmas tree may be the answer. And since buying one is a long-term investment, it’s important to purchase one you love that also works in your space. For those who don’t want to deal with a real tree, I talked to experts about how to shop for a quality artificial Christmas tree and rounded up some of the best options based on their advice. I also asked experts about the environmental impact of Christmas trees, and what those with allergies and pets specifically should be aware of before buying one. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. The best artificial Christmas trees Below, I rounded up highly-rated artificial Christmas trees based on expert guidance. I made sure to include options across price points, sizes and styles, and separated unlit and pre-lit options. To help you determine how full each tree is, we note the trees’ tip count (meaning branch tips) if provided by the brand. The higher the tip count, the fuller the tree will look. I also point out if the tree comes in one, display-ready piece (pre-assembled) or not. All of the options below have at least a 4-star average rating from 100 reviews or more on one of the retailer websites. Best pre-lit artificial Christmas trees Best pre-lit compact tree This tree, available in a space-conscious size, and comes recommended by NBC Selected reporter Zoe Malin. “It gives me plenty of room to spread out my ornaments , but isn’t so big that it’s intimidating to put together or take apart,” she says. “It’s quite sturdy, too. I love that it comes pre-lit, which prevents me from having to wrestle with string lights. I can’t wait to set it up again this year.” Best pre-lit spruce-style tree The North Valley Spruce tree from National Tree Company stands over 7 feet tall, making it perfect for those who have high ceilings and want to fill out their living room with a festive tree. It has a 52-inch base diameter, so it’s less likely to wobble, even as you decorate it. The branches, which resemble those of traditional spruce trees, are easy to fluff outward for a full look, but they also fold back inward for quick storage. Best pre-lit alpine-style tree If you’re looking for a slim option that resembles an alpine fir tree, this pick from Balsam Hill is designed with tight spaces in mind, according to the brand. It’s pre-lit with LED fairy lights and available in six heights. Sparse by design, this balsam-style tree’s faux trunk is visible through the branches and the tree’s foliage is frosted to mimic snow. Plus, it comes with extra bulbs. Best pre-lit tabletop tree This tiny but festive pre-lit tree also comes recommended by Malin, who typically displays it on her dining table or coffee table. “The rainbow lights add color, so I usually don’t decorate this tree other than adding a little topper,” she says. “It doesn’t take up much room in my home and is very easy to store,” she says. It has 71 branch tips and 35 multicolor lights, plus a decorated red and gold stand. Best tree with multiple lighting effects This eclectic pre-lit Christmas tree comes studded with mini pine cones on the end of each branch. It’s also pre-flocked, so it looks lightly dusted with snow for a more authentic look. Depending on which size you get, the tree has up to 700 warm white light bulbs to compliment your adornments. Best unlit artificial Christmas trees Best overall unlit tree Available in three models, this spruce-like tree has a built-in foldable base and a full shape. With a 4.6-star average rating from over 15,000 shoppers on Amazon, this tree can handle a range of ornaments and different light styles, such as fairy or vintage. Best unlit tabletop tree Available in either 2- or 3-foot options, this mini tree can be a festive centerpiece for dining or coffee tables, or you could simply place it on your dresser or mantle next to stockings. You can also decorate it with mini ornaments or a short string of battery-operated fairy lights. It also has a durable round cement base wrapped in a festive cloth, and 67 branch tips. Best unlit tree worth the splurge This eye-catching, realistic-looking tree is available in several sizes and lighting styles, including unlit. Thanks to its full silhouette, it’s an ideal foundation for large ornaments, garland, tinsels, festive steamers and a topper of your choice. How I picked the best artificial Christmas trees Here are the expert-recommended factors I kept in mind while making this list: Height: Since everyone’s ceilings have different dimensions, I made sure to include artificial Christmas trees with a range of heights, from 4 feet up to 15 feet. Pre-lit vs. unlit: Our list includes pre-lit trees and unlit trees. Pre-lit trees are often more expensive than unlit ones. Lighting effects: For those who want a pre-lit tree, it’s also important to choose a tree with lighting effects that match the tone of your space. Consider whether that means a tree with either one or multiple colors, or with twinkly options. Some of the pre-lit trees below have twinkling effects as well as multiple color options. Storage options: Artificial trees typically come in a box broken down and with branches compressed to help make it easier to store. How you receive the tree is typically how you’ll have to store it when the holidays are over. Be sure to consider whether you have a large enough closet or storage space in your home. How to shop for an artificial Christmas tree Since Christmas trees become part of your home decor for weeks (or months, depending on when you put yours up), purchasing one is largely about your personal style preferences. You’ll want to consider the following factors: Size: Artificial Christmas trees come in a variety of sizes — some are over 12 feet tall, while others are smaller, allowing you to put them on tabletops. Before you purchase a tree, decide where you want to put it and what size would work best for that area. Plus, if you choose a tree on the taller side, you may need a stepping stool when it comes time to decorate it. Color: Some people want to find the most realistic looking artificial tree possible and opt for green varieties. If you want a non-traditional route, you can find trees in neon colors, white, black and other shades. They typically come in a traditional warm white light, while others have more shades. Plus, you’ll want to make sure you have an appropriate place for storage before you buy one: While you may be able to display a 12-foot tree in your living room during the holidays, your closet may not be able to accommodate that same size, even once it’s disassembled. articles.title: A Utah man cut down his neighbour’s mature trees with a tractor, arguing that a historic easement allowed him to build an access road; repeated clashes led to a stalking injunction
articles.summary: A disagreement over access to private land in Utah escalated after a man used a tractor to clear mature trees on his neighbour’s property, arguing that an
articles.body: A disagreement over access to private land in Utah escalated after a man used a tractor to clear mature trees on his neighbour’s property, arguing that an old easement gave him a route to reach his own land. The dispute eventually involved more than the question of where a road could be built. The neighbour sought a civil stalking injunction, and the courts had to consider whether conduct linked to a property disagreement could justify restrictions intended to protect an individual. The Utah Court of Appeals dated May 2026 upheld the injunction against the man, while a separate civil case over the disputed easement remained unresolved. The ruling also examined how quickly courts must hear challenges to such orders.Utah land access dispute escalates after alleged property damageThe case, Hasemeyer v. LeFevre, concerned neighbours living in a rural part of southern Utah. Matthew LeFevre believed a historic easement crossed the northern edge of Eric Hasemeyer’s property and would allow him to reach an undeveloped section of his own land. He wanted to use that route to build an access road, with plans to develop the land for a house.Hasemeyer disputed that interpretation. An easement had historically existed in the area, but the neighbours disagreed over whether it remained valid and where it ran. Access to the disputed route was also complicated by a locked county gate. The court did not settle the ownership and access question in the stalking proceedings; that issue was being pursued separately.The disagreement became more serious in October 2024. LeFevre asked Hasemeyer for a key to the county gate without explaining why he needed it. After handing over the key, Hasemeyer noticed trees falling near the back of his property. He went to investigate and found that LeFevre had used a tractor to destroy two or three mature trees, according to the Utah Court of Appeals’ account of the evidence.When Hasemeyer challenged him, LeFevre said he was removing the trees because he had an easement. He stopped the work after the confrontation, but the incident prompted Hasemeyer to seek legal advice.On 16 October 2024, Hasemeyer’s lawyer sent LeFevre a cease-and-desist letter. The lawyer said an initial review of the property deeds and related records suggested that the claimed easement did not exist, while a formal title search was still being pursued. The letter demanded that LeFevre stop trespassing and causing further damage.Utah easement dispute intensifies after more trees are removedThe first confrontation did not settle the matter. LeFevre later sent Hasemeyer a survey document that he believed supported his claim to the route. Reportedly, on 7 November 2024, he returned to the disputed area with heavy equipment, apparently the same tractor, and removed more trees and shrubs while beginning to grade a road.The neighbours remained at odds over the documents. In February 2025, LeFevre emailed Hasemeyer to ask about the response to the material he had provided. The following day, Hasemeyer’s lawyer sent another letter, arguing that any easement LeFevre held ran through the southern part of the property, not the northern section where the trees had been removed. The lawyer again demanded that he stop the work.A further confrontation followed on 26 February 2025. Hasemeyer’s wife was working in a greenhouse at the northern end of the property when she saw LeFevre operating his truck and tractor. As he approached the disputed route, she stepped onto the path in front of him.According to the evidence later considered by the court, LeFevre continued moving slowly until the tractor was immediately in front of her legs. She told him to stay off the property. He laughed and left, taking a county road back to his house rather than using the disputed route.The encounter did not end there. Hasemeyer had witnessed part of it from inside the house and called 911. Before officers arrived, LeFevre returned to the area with a blade extension attached to his tractor. His neighbour’s wife recorded the second approach on her phone. She testified that he turned quickly onto the disputed route and came towards her at speed, lifting the tractor’s blade as he advanced. She had to step backwards to avoid him before he stopped.Utah court weighs stalking injunction amid a disputed property easementHasemeyer sought a civil stalking injunction after the incidents. The request was not simply about the loss of trees or the construction of an unwanted road. It also relied on the repeated entries onto the property and the February encounters involving the tractor and Hasemeyer’s wife.The court initially granted an injunction without first hearing from LeFevre. Such an order is known as an ex parte injunction. LeFevre challenged it and requested an evidentiary hearing, at which both sides could present their accounts and supporting material.During the hearing, the parties offered documents relating to the disputed easement as well as evidence about the three incidents. LeFevre maintained that he was trying to reach his own land, not harass or threaten his neighbours. He argued that he genuinely believed he had a legal right to use the route and that a stalking injunction was an unsuitable way to resolve a property dispute.Appeals court rejects challenge to stalking injunction over disputed Utah landLeFevre appealed to the Utah Court of Appeals, arguing that his actions did not amount to stalking, the evidentiary hearing was delayed improperly, the pending easement lawsuit prevented the injunction, and its restrictions were too broad.The court rejected his main arguments, finding that the repeated property entries, tree removal and tractor encounters supported the injunction under Utah’s stalking law. Judge Ryan D. Tenney, who wrote the opinion, added a section on his own behalf (Part I(C)), which the two other judges, Gregory K. Orme and Ryan M. Harris did not join.In it he suggested that Utah Supreme Court precedent on when conduct is ‘directed at’ an individual should be reexamined. He acknowledged, however, that the result was compelled by existing caselaw, and the injunction was upheld.The court also examined the delay in the hearingLeFevre had requested an evidentiary hearing on 10 March 2025, three days after the initial injunction was issued. The district court held an initial hearing on 24 March, heard evidence on 7 April and received closing arguments on 21 April. The final ruling therefore came 42 days after his request.Utah law generally requires an evidentiary hearing within ten days of a respondent's written request, unless compelling reasons justify a delay. The appellate court agreed that the statute referred to an evidentiary hearing, not simply any court appearance. It also accepted that scheduling pressures could amount to compelling reasons in certain circumstances.The judges said courts should weigh the reasons for a delay against the prejudice it causes the person subject to the injunction. The length of the delay and the importance of the restrictions also matter. In this case, the injunction did not prevent LeFevre from accessing his home or workplace, although it prevented him from entering his neighbour's property to use the disputed route. The court found no reversible error in the delay.The easement question remains unresolvedThe appeal did not determine whether LeFevre had a valid easement across the northern part of Hasemeyer's land. The court declined to consider his argument that a pending civil lawsuit over the route legally barred the stalking injunction because he had not properly raised that issue in the lower court. It also rejected his challenge to the injunction's scope. The order barred him from entering Hasemeyer's home, premises or property for a period of three years. Although LeFevre argued that this effectively prevented him from exercising the access rights he claimed, the court said the restrictions were within the district court's discretion under the circumstances. The judges noted that if LeFevre succeeds in the separate easement litigation, he can ask the court to modify or revoke the injunction. For now, the restrictions remain in place.You use AI every day. articles.title: Landline switchover could cut people off in emergency, minister warned
articles.summary: Plans to switch to digital landlines by January could leave remote areas of the UK vulnerable, MPs say.
articles.body:
Plans to switch off the UK's traditional landline phone network could leave people in remote areas unable to contact help in an emergency, MPs have warned.

Landline operators aim to complete the switch to an internet-based network instead of copper-wire cables by the end of January next year.

The government and operators say the move to digital landlines will offer a more reliable service.

But MPs representing remote areas of the UK urged security minister Dan Jarvis to ensure that scrapping the copper-wire network did not make their communities more vulnerable in a storm or other emergency.

Unlike digital services, the traditional landline network does not rely on mains electricity and continues to work in a power cut.

Labour MP Torcuil Crichton, who represents the Western Isles constituency of Na h-Eileanan an Iar, said: "Resilience is inbuilt in the islands but we have major problems with connectivity because of this move from analogue to digital phone lines."

He said that "when the power goes out people don't have the phone, they don't have the internet and often they don't have a mobile signal either".

BT OpenReach has been giving back-up battery packs to vulnerable customers, which can keep landline phones operating for an hour or more.

But Crichton said this was "simply not adequate" and that mobile phone providers "simply don't have the means to maintain or keep their signal going during storms".

He urged the minister to get telecoms firms to "up their digital game" to protect places "on the edge where people are vulnerable, isolated from their neighbours, where the ambulance is an hour away and the storm is 70 miles an hour".

Similar concerns were raised by MPs from the West Country and the Lake District.

Markus Campbell-Savours, Labour MP for Penrith and Solway, said: "I ask the minister to imagine an elderly constituent living alone in an isolated Lake District valley where copper phone lines have been replaced by fibre.

"A storm takes out the power to their router in the night and by the time they wake, the modest battery back up has failed, as has the mobile mast, does the minister share my concerns that they would have no way to raise an alarm in an emergency and agree that we need a new technological solution to protect the elderly?"

'We won't be able to use our phones if we have a power cut'

Switchover must protect most vulnerable - MPs

Conservative MP Julian Lewis also raised concerns about the lack of a "back-up system" if digital phone services go down in the event of a cyber attack or other emergency.

He told Jarvis the copper-wire network "could have given us useful levels of resilience in an emergency".

Jarvis, who is spearheading the government's Be Ready campaign, which is advising people to stock up on supplies to be prepared for emergencies , said he would "look very closely" at the Tory MP's point.

He also assured West Country MPs that their concerns would be addressed at a government resilience summit, which was due to take place in Cornwall next month, and promised to raise concerns about telecoms firms with the Department for Culture, Media and Sport.

"Our telephone networks are a vital part of our critical national infrastructure and our emergency response in weather-related crisis supports the functioning of essential services and keeping people connected when they need it most," he told MPs.

The government says the switch to digital phone services is needed because the traditional analogue network is becoming increasingly unreliable.

The government's Be Ready campaign advises people who have not yet "migrated to a modern digital network" to contact their landline provider.

"If you are a vulnerable customer, for example if you are a telecare user, your communication provider must provide a free back‑up battery unit," it adds.

More information is available on the government's digital switchover site .

articles.title: Ghanaian twins and US woman plead guilty to romance scams
articles.summary: The group targeted elderly people across US and Europe, luring them into romantic relationship before persuading them to transfer large sums of money.
articles.body:
Twin brothers from Ghana and an American woman have pleaded guilty to being part of an international criminal network that defrauded people on dating sites and social media.

The group targeted elderly people in the US and Europe, using fake identities to lure their victims into believing they were in a romantic relationship, before persuading them to transfer large sums of money into bank accounts in Ghana.

The 22-year-old twins, Jamal and Kamal Abubakari, and 53-year-old Amanda Joy Opoku-Boachie from Hawaii face up to 20 years in jail and will be sentenced next year.

Between July 2024 - April 2026, the victims collectively lost $9m (£6.7m).

While many of them were from Ohio - where the charges were brought - other victims were located in 24 other US states, as well as Germany and Austria.

As part of the plea, the Abubakaris and Opoku-Boachie agreed to forfeit pieces of jewellery which investigators seized during their arrest, including luxury watches, rings, chains and earrings.

Jamal Abubakari, also known as Jamal Abubakar and Arrangement

Kamal Abubakari, also known as Kamal Abubakar and Lancaster

Joy Opoku-Boachie, also known as Amanda Joy Glum and Amanda Joy Kessei Bierman

In recent months, US authorities have stepped up their crackdown on criminal networks operating in the US and West Africa which seek to defraud elderly Americans.

Earlier this month, FBI Director Kash Patel said it had made hundreds of arrests after dismantling a scam centre in Ghana.

In June, a Ghanaian social media influencer known as Abu Trica, whose real name is Frederick Kumi, was extradited to the US to face trial for allegedly running a romance scam that defrauded elderly Americans of more than $8m (£5.9m).

He targeted victims through social media and online dating platforms, and is accused of requesting money or valuables under false pretences such as urgent medical needs.

The case against Kumi is being prosecuted under the US Elder Abuse Prevention and Prosecution law. He denies all the charges against him.

articles.summary: Flavio Bolsonaro has left Brazil for the U.S. after losing the presidential election and refusing to comply with a court order ⁠to hand over his passports.
articles.body: Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro has left the country for the United States after losing Sunday’s presidential election and refusing to comply with a Supreme Court order ⁠to hand over his passports, two sources said. The U.S. Embassy in Brazil did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Bolsonaro’s lawyer also declined to comment. Bolsonaro was favored to win Sunday’s presidential election but ended up losing in a shock result ⁠to leftist incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da ​Silva. ⁠On Monday, he was given 24 hours to hand in his passports as part of a money laundering probe in which ⁠he denies wrongdoing, but that deadline has now lapsed, two other sources said, ​leading ⁠to his documents being canceled. Flavio’s ‌father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, also went to the United States after refusing to concede losing to Lula in 2022. He eventually returned to Brazil ‌but was later given a 27-year sentence for plotting ‌a coup. His son has yet to officially concede defeat — saying on Sunday he would seek the annulment of the result over alleged voter irregularities — but his Liberal Party said ⁠on Monday it acknowledged Lula’s victory. A senior Brazilian Federal Police official said Bolsonaro has not exited the country via any regular migration point. Right-wing influencer Paulo Figueiredo, who serves as a sort of unofficial spokesperson for the Bolsonaro family, declined to answer questions about Bolsonaro’s whereabouts. “After months of intense work that has been unfairly thwarted, I am not in the mood to ‌speak to the press,” he said in a message. “If I have ​any comments to make on any matter, I will get in ‌touch.” Eduardo Bolsonaro, Bolsonaro’s younger brother ⁠who lives in the United States, said ahead of the vote ⁠that an election loss would require a move. “If my brother does not win, I’m in ‌favor that he would leave ​the country,” he told podcaster Steven ‌Crowder this month.

articles.title: An Australian homeowner said water from an uphill neighbour's blocked drainage pipe flooded his backyard and pool; a court awarded A$99,382 in damages, and a 2026 appeals court upheld the ruling and repair order
articles.summary: An Australian homeowner has won a long legal battle against his uphill neighbour after faulty drainage repeatedly sent water into his backyard and damaged
articles.body: An Australian homeowner has won a long legal battle against his uphill neighbour after faulty drainage repeatedly sent water into his backyard and damaged his swimming pool. The New South Wales Court of Appeal upheld a district court ruling that found the owners of the higher property responsible for the damage. The court ordered them to pay A$99,382.01 (£51,200) in compensation and complete repairs to fix their stormwater drainage system. The dispute involved Charbel Tannous, who owns the lower property, and his uphill neighbours, Ya Jun Tang and his co-owners. The case focused on repeated flooding caused by water flowing from the higher land into Mr Tannous's home.Blocked pipes trigger backyard floodingAccording to court documents published by the Supreme Court of New South Wales under appeal docket 2026/00016256, the flooding was linked to a drainage easement on the higher property. Mr Tannous claimed that Mr Tang and his family had failed to maintain and repair the stormwater drainage system serving their land. Over time, an underground pipe became misshapen and blocked, stopping rainwater from flowing away as it should. During heavy rain, excess water spilled over the boundary from the higher property and flowed directly onto Mr Tannous's lower lot. The repeated flooding covered his lawn, filled his backyard with water, and carried debris into his swimming pool. This contaminated the pool water and caused structural damage. Despite repeated complaints, the problem continued. Mr Tannous eventually filed a private nuisance lawsuit in the New South Wales District Court.District court awards damages and repair mandateDuring the trial in the New South Wales District Court, Judge Cole heard Mr Tang deny responsibility for the water damage. The defence argued that building work on Mr Tannous's property had caused the flooding. This included excavation, demolition, and the removal of an existing concrete kerb. Mr Tang also filed a cross-claim under Section 177 of the Conveyancing Act 1919. He argued that Mr Tannous's construction work had weakened the structural support for the higher property. Judge Cole rejected the defence arguments and dismissed the cross-claim entirely. The court found that the misshapen and blocked stormwater pipe on the higher property was the main cause of the repeated flooding. The district court ruled that the uphill owners had created a private nuisance by failing to fix their faulty drainage system. Judge Cole ordered them to pay Mr Tannous A$99,382.01 in compensation. The judge also issued a mandatory court order requiring Mr Tang to repair and redesign the drainage system to prevent water from flowing onto the lower property again.Appeals court rejects challenge to rulingMr Tang and his co-owners sought to overturn the decision. In March 2026, they applied to the New South Wales Court of Appeal for permission to challenge the ruling. The compensation award was just below the A$100,000 limit required for an automatic right of appeal under Section 127(2)(c) of the District Court Act 1973. The applicants therefore needed formal permission from the appeals court to proceed. In legal submissions prepared by their lawyer, M. Luitingh, the applicants argued that the trial judge had made several factual errors about the removal of the kerb. They also claimed that the judge had relied on assumptions about their motives rather than physical evidence. They further argued that the order requiring repairs was legally flawed. They said that changing the pipe's layout required approval from the local municipal council, which could make it impossible to carry out the court's instructions. M. Young SC, representing Mr Tannous, argued that the trial judge had applied the law correctly. He said the evidence clearly showed that the failure to address the blocked pipe had caused a private nuisance. The appeals court upheld the original decision. It agreed that the trial judge had correctly identified the blocked pipe as the main cause of the flooding. The court also confirmed that owners of higher properties have a legal duty to prevent foreseeable water runoff caused by neglected drainage systems on their land. The ruling leaves the original A$99,382.01 compensation award unchanged. It also requires the uphill owners to complete the ordered drainage repairs.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Alex Pretti’s family says feds are still stonewalling efforts for justice
articles.summary: The parents of Alex Pretti, a US citizen shot and killed by immigration agents in Minneapolis in January, are accusing the Department of Justice of violating...
articles.body:
PROGRAMMING NOTE: Susan and Michael Pretti join CNN's Jake Tapper on The Lead at 5 p.m. Eastern

The parents of Alex Pretti , a US citizen shot and killed by immigration agents in Minneapolis in January, are accusing the Department of Justice of violating their rights under a federal victims' rights law, as they demand transparency and justice in their son's death.

In a July letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche — obtained exclusively by CNN — an attorney representing Michael and Susan Pretti wrote they have not received any substantive updates from the DOJ regarding an investigation into their son's death, and called the department's attitude toward the case "cruel."

"The government's pattern of conduct is not only unconscionable, but unlawful," the letter states.

Pretti's parents on Tuesday accused the federal government of "shielding Alex's killers" by not turning over the entire federal case file to state investigators.

"We will no longer stay silent about the actions of the Department of Justice in the 275 days since Alex's murder," Pretti's father, Michael, said in the family's first news conference since the 37-year-old ICU nurse's death.

The Pretti family met with US Attorney for the District of Minnesota Dan Rosen on July 13, the letter explains, the same day Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced in a news conference federal officials had handed over volumes of evidence from Pretti's shooting.

However, the letter goes on to say that, despite a public acknowledgment from local officials of an evidence-sharing agreement, Rosen refused to provide any information and would not even confirm the arrangement.

"It is impossible to convey how the government's refusal to engage in transparent communication with the Pretti family has compounded their heartbreak," the missive says.

"Further, with each such refusal, U.S. Attorney Rosen even refused to explain the basis for his position, instead stating only that 'I can't tell you for all kinds of reasons,' without providing a single one," according to the letter.

Federal investigators who briefly agreed to share their evidence with state law enforcement have since stopped cooperating , said Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, who is leading a lawsuit against the Department of Justice.

"We are in litigation with the federal government right now to secure the rest of the remaining file, which they could give us this morning if they were inclined to do so, but it looks like we're going to need a court order. I'm sorry that it comes to that," Ellison told CNN's Sara Sidner Tuesday morning. "Any prosecutor can tell you, you can't go forward with half a file. You need the whole thing."

CNN has reached out to the DOJ and the US Attorney for Minnesota.

In its response to Minnesota's lawsuit, the Department of Justice said it is not required to turn over evidence to a state agency before an active court case is underway.

The Pretti family's attorney, Steve Schleicher, says they have heard nothing from the DOJ since sending their letter.

"I've never seen a family treated with such cruelty and disrespect," he said.

Pretti's death was captured in its entirety on video. Like some other incidents that occurred as a result of the Trump administration's ongoing immigration crackdown, the footage from Pretti's shooting differed from the version of events provided by the Department of Homeland Security.

Kristi Noem, then-DHS secretary, initially described Pretti as a "terrorist" who "attacked" officers after "brandishing" a weapon, though the video disputed those claims. White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller referred to Pretti as an "assassin" who tried to murder federal agents.

"No one from the federal government called us on that horrible day, but they did go on TV to tell lies about Alex," Michael Pretti said Tuesday.

Video footage shows, minutes before the fatal encounter with Pretti, immigration agents patrolling a Minneapolis street and interacting with bystanders. A witness, Nilson Barahona, told CNN agents were trying to apprehend someone who fled into a donut shop that locked its doors, leaving the group of federal officers on the sidewalk and street. Agents detained one observer as others blew whistles, yelled and recorded video on their phones.

Video shows Pretti attempting to intervene in a scuffle between an observer and the agents.

During the incident, Pretti was pepper-sprayed in the face. One of the officers can be heard in the footage shouting: "Gun! Gun! Gun!" as Pretti is on his knees and bent forward. An agent removed Pretti's gun from his waistband and can be seen exiting the skirmish. At about the same time, one agent drew his service weapon.

About a second after the agent holding Pretti's weapon moved away, the officer who drew his own weapon appeared to fire several shots at Pretti before another agent drew his weapon and a shot rang out. The other officer then raised his gun and fired more shots. At least 10 gunshots can be heard on the video.

The DHS report on its initial investigation into Pretti's death says an officer yelled, "He's got a gun" multiple times before the officers fired.

"It's difficult to get up every day, to function, to be a parent, knowing that your child's never coming home," Susan Pretti told CNN's Jake Tapper after Tuesday's news conference. "No parent should have to live what we're living. No daughter should have to wake up and know that her only sibling is no longer here."

"What the federal government has taken away from us, from his friends, his family, his colleagues, from his patients, from the patients' families. They've taken away all of that — and it's reprehensible," he told Tapper.

Susan Pretti said she knew Alex as her son, but the outpouring of support they've received from his friends and coworkers has helped her see another side of him.

"Every letter and card that we received from his colleagues, telling us who he was, at work … not only helping his patients but his colleagues," Susan Pretti said, choking up. "You know what that's like for a parent to hear? It is probably the kindest thing a parent can ever hear about their child."

Michael Pretti said his trust in the government is fading.

Pretti's death followed the fatal shooting of Renee Good on January 7 and the non-fatal shooting of Julio Sosa-Celis on January 14 by immigration agents during Operation Metro Surge. Those incidents prompted significant protests in Minneapolis and across the country for weeks.

Hennepin County prosecutors have fought the DOJ for key evidence in Pretti's death for months, after federal law enforcement repeatedly threw up blockades to their access.

On the day Pretti was killed, the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension attempted to access the scene to launch an investigation but was banned by federal authorities. CNN was on scene the next day when the BCA first accessed the scene on a court order from a state judge.

State and local investigators sued the Trump administration in federal court to obtain evidence in Pretti's killing. After an evidence-sharing agreement between the DOJ and Minnesota investigators was finalized in June, Hennepin County prosecutors received volumes of evidence in Pretti's shooting.

Weeks later, the DOJ abruptly changed course and stopped sharing information, leaving Hennepin County prosecutors unable to access crucial evidence such as the weapons used to shoot Pretti and the firearm Pretti was carrying in his waistband at the time of the altercation, according to court records filed October 13.

The letter from Pretti's parents asks the DOJ to identify the federal employees who shot and killed Pretti, commit to sharing information with state and local investigators, confirm whether the FBI is continuing to investigate Pretti's murder, and return any items of Pretti's personal property no longer needed for evidentiary purposes.

"No family should have to beg the U.S. government to do its job," the letter says. "And no government should act with such caprice."

The Pretti family's attorney declined to say Tuesday whether they would file a suit of their own against the Department of Justice.

"The family will avail itself to any and all remedies in its pursuit of justice for Alex," Schleicher said.

Until they find justice, the family is comforted by shared memories of their son. Michael Pretti recalled a specific camping trip when Alex was about 6 years old. Just as they were wrapping up the weekend and preparing to leave, Alex rode his new bike off a small bridge and into a creek.

"He comes back and he's soaked," Michael Pretti said with a grin, prompting a chuckle from his wife. "That was a good memory, that was a good weekend that stands out," he said, adding "that's probably where his love for hiking and biking started."

CNN's Andy Rose and Cindy Von Quednow contributed to this report.

For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com
